# Omni View Top World News
> **Two crossings shut as Baghdad took Kurdish oilfields and Trump backed the seizure.**

**What You Need to Know:** Two crossings shut as Baghdad took Kurdish oilfields and Trump backed the seizure, ahead of Baghdad–Erbil talks set for December 1. Washington’s first comment on that rift followed a court ruling that lets federal forces deploy on every Iraqi border, including the Kurdish region’s. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Why is Trump backing Iraq’s anti-smuggling campaign?: Al Jazeera**
Iraq’s federal government spent this week pulling oil routes, border gates and armed groups toward Baghdad, and the United States president put his name on that campaign before a dialogue with the Kurdish region that is already on the calendar.

The public American turn came on Friday. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social: “We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state.” A second sentence in the same post said, “We support Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions.” Al Jazeera reported that the post was Washington’s first comment on the tensions between Baghdad and Erbil. It arrived days before talks between the two, due on December 1 under the sponsorship of the head of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council.

The week’s operational sequence, as Al Jazeera lays it out, is short and dated. On Tuesday, al-Zaidi moved to place the Kurdish region’s border crossings and several oilfields under federal control. On Wednesday, Iraq’s top court ruled that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all of the country’s international borders, including those of the Kurdish region. On Thursday, Iraq closed two crossings in that region, one with Syria and one with Iran. France 24 described the prime minister as taking bold steps to curb rampant oil smuggling, moves the United States has praised, and steps that risk putting him at odds with Iraq’s Kurds and with neighbouring Iran. The French account does not add a separate casualty figure, a named field, or a quoted Kurdish reply. The American post, on Al Jazeera’s reading, is the first Washington comment after those measures, not a new operational order of its own.

Salim Zakhour, a researcher specialising in constitutional law and political systems, told Al Jazeera the timing is significant because Trump’s post comes after Baghdad’s measures and before the planned dialogue. “It is a clear message, first to the federal government, as a show of support for it,” he said. “But the more important message is for the authorities and Kurdish leaders in the Kurdistan region. It tells them that all the measures taken by the federal government have strong American backing.” That is an analyst’s account of who the post is aimed at. Trump’s own sentences name four aims in one breath: state authority throughout Iraq, a stop to smuggling of Iraqi oil, an end to corruption, and weapons under the exclusive control of the state.

Baghdad’s stated reason is the treasury. The Iraqi government says it wants to clamp down on oil smuggling that is harming its economy. Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi told the Iraqi News Agency that Iraq has lost an estimated $100 billion between 2008 and 2025 from oil smuggled through the Kurdish region. That number is the government’s estimate, given by its spokesperson to the state news agency, and carried by Al Jazeera. It covers seventeen years and a route the government says ran through the semi-autonomous region, not a single seizure announced this week.

The campaign did not open on the Kurdish frontier. Al Jazeera reports that it began in Jurf al-Sakhar, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, a town in Babil province south of Baghdad. The armed group Kataib Hezbollah has held the town since 2014, when Iran-backed groups took it from ISIL, also called ISIS. Its mostly Sunni residents were displaced. Al Jazeera describes Kataib Hezbollah as Iran’s most powerful armed ally in Iraq. The United States designates the group a terrorist organisation. The group denies the allegations.

Senior Iraqi security, army, police and oil officials told the Reuters news agency that Kataib Hezbollah has since run an oil smuggling network there, siphoning off state-owned crude worth hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021. Those are allegations from officials, relayed by Reuters and reported by Al Jazeera. They are not a court finding in these articles. Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed and referred to the courts. Referral is the step the reports record. They do not record a verdict against those nine.

Al-Zaidi gave the group until November 20 to leave the town. A day before the deadline, the two sides reached a compromise, reportedly following direct intervention by Esmail Qaani, the head of Iran’s Quds Force. Under the deal, government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar and set up a joint operations centre. Kataib Hezbollah units are due to withdraw gradually as army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilisation Forces units deploy in phases. The articles describe an agreed sequence and an entry already made. They describe the armed units’ exit as due, and gradual, as those other units deploy.

Kataib Hezbollah is not the only group resisting Baghdad’s push to bring weapons under state control. Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have also refused to disarm. After the armed groups missed a September 30 deadline to hand over their weapons to the state, the government pushed the deadline to June 2027. Two clocks now sit side by side. One is local: a phased entry in Babil after a compromise reached the day before November 20, with Iran’s Quds Force chief reported as the intervener. The other is national: a weapons date the government itself moved from the end of September to June 2027 after groups did not meet the first date. Trump’s Friday sentence folds both kinds of aim into one endorsement — oil smuggling stopped, and all weapons under exclusive state control — without setting either clock.

Baghdad then extended the campaign from that town to the Kurdish region. The extension, in the reporting, is concrete: border crossings and several oilfields placed under a federal claim on Tuesday; a top-court ruling on Wednesday that federal forces may deploy on every international border, including the Kurdish region’s; two closures on Thursday, one gate with Syria and one with Iran. The people the week changes something for are not one bloc. Kurdish authorities face federal claims on crossings and fields they had been running inside a semi-autonomous region, with a dialogue dated for Monday under the head of the Supreme Judicial Council. Traders and officials who used the two closed gates face a shut frontier on two sides of the region at once. Armed groups that have refused to disarm face a stated federal aim, now echoed by the American president, that weapons sit only with the state, against a deadline already slipped to June 2027. Residents of Jurf al-Sakhar live with a joint operations centre in a town held since 2014, after officials told Reuters that state crude was siphoned there; the group that held the town denies that account. Mostly Sunni residents of the town were displaced when Iran-backed groups took it from ISIL. Iran appears twice in these reports: as the neighbour France 24 says Baghdad risks clashing with, and as the state whose Quds Force chief is reported to have stepped in so a compromise could be reached before the November 20 deadline.

What the Friday post changes, on the evidence these articles actually give, is the diplomatic frame for December 1, not a completed transfer of fields and not a finished disarmament. Zakhour’s point is that Kurdish leaders are being shown American backing for measures already taken, before they sit down. Trump’s words set the four aims. He did not, in the text Al Jazeera quotes, describe the two closed crossings or the $100 billion estimate. The operational steps named in the reporting are al-Zaidi’s: Tuesday’s move on crossings and oilfields, Wednesday’s court ruling as the legal step Baghdad can cite, Thursday’s closures, the Jurf al-Sakhar entry, the referral of nine officials to the courts, and the June 2027 weapons date.

The next dated step these articles name for the Kurdish dispute is December 1. The next dated step they name for weapons is June 2027. Between those dates, the Babil compromise still has Kataib Hezbollah units withdrawing only as army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilisation Forces units deploy in phases. The government’s loss figure remains an estimate spoken by Haider al-Aboudi to the Iraqi News Agency, attached to oil the government says was smuggled through the region from 2008 to 2025. The hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021 remain an allegation from senior Iraqi officials to Reuters, denied by the group the United States designates a terrorist organisation. France 24’s risk line — at odds with Iraq’s Kurds and with Iran — sits next to an American endorsement that arrived after the closures and before the talks.

Ranks: Kurdish authorities, border trade and armed groups across Iraq · federal claims on oilfields, two closed crossings and a weapons monopoly, still incomplete · talks December 1, weapons deadline June 2027 Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/why-is-trump-backing-iraqs-anti-smuggling-campaign)
Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/syrian-kurds-protest-against-baghdad-leader-s-moves-to-assert-central-control)

### Both Sides: Federal control of Kurdish oil routes and weapons
Iraq’s government is deciding how far Baghdad, rather than the Kurdish region or armed groups, will run international borders, oilfields and weapons. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has already moved crossings and several oilfields toward federal control, closed two regional crossings, and set a state monopoly on arms as policy. President Donald Trump has endorsed that package in a Truth Social post. Talks with Erbil are due on December 1 under the head of the Supreme Judicial Council. A separate weapons deadline now sits at June 2027, after groups missed September 30.

The case for exclusive federal control, as al-Zaidi’s government and Trump state it, starts with the treasury and the state’s claim to force. The government says oil smuggling is harming the economy. Spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi told the Iraqi News Agency the loss through the Kurdish region is an estimated $100 billion from 2008 to 2025. Senior Iraqi security, army, police and oil officials told Reuters that a network in Jurf al-Sakhar, also called Jurf al-Nasr, siphoned state-owned crude worth hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021. Trump’s post ties that crackdown to a second aim: all weapons under the exclusive control of the state, corruption ended, and an Iraq that “makes its own political decisions.” Iraq’s top court has ruled that Baghdad may deploy federal forces on all international borders, including the Kurdish region’s. Salim Zakhour told Al Jazeera the American post is a show of support for the federal government and a message to Kurdish leaders that the measures already taken have strong American backing. A supporter of the push can point to a court ruling, a dated loss estimate from the government spokesperson, allegations from senior officials, referrals to the courts, and an American endorsement before Monday’s talks.

The case against treating those steps as settled starts with denial, refusal, and the risk of a wider rift. Kataib Hezbollah, which the United States designates a terrorist organisation and which Al Jazeera calls Iran’s most powerful armed ally in Iraq, denies the smuggling allegations. The group has held Jurf al-Sakhar since 2014, when Iran-backed groups took it from ISIL, and its mostly Sunni residents were displaced. The government already moved its weapons deadline from September 30 to June 2027 after groups missed the first date. A compromise in Jurf al-Sakhar, reportedly after intervention by Esmail Qaani, head of Iran’s Quds Force, has government forces inside the town with a joint operations centre, and Kataib Hezbollah units leaving only gradually as army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilisation Forces units deploy in phases. France 24 reports that the smuggling crackdown, which the United States has praised, risks putting al-Zaidi at odds with Iraq’s Kurds and with neighbouring Iran. On Zakhour’s reading, Kurdish leaders are being shown that Washington backs measures taken before they sit down on December 1. The $100 billion figure is the federal spokesperson’s estimate. The hundreds of millions are allegations officials gave Reuters, which the accused group denies. Thursday’s two closures — one crossing with Syria, one with Iran — are federal acts taken before the dialogue, not a joint decision announced with Erbil.

What happens next is dated, not decided. The weapons handover date the government now cites is June 2027. The phased withdrawal in Babil is still described as due, not done. Trump’s post names the aims.

### Progress Watch
The World Health Organization said on Friday that global measles deaths hit a historic low in 2025. The UN health agency estimated 9.8 million measles cases and about 72,000 deaths worldwide in 2025, down 74 percent from 37.8 million cases in 2000, with deaths falling roughly 91 percent from about 769,000. The same account says millions of children still missed vaccinations and that outbreaks persisted in dozens of countries. The measured drop is the result the agency published. The missed vaccinations and the outbreaks in dozens of countries are the limit that account places on the same fight. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/world-health-organization-sounds-alarm-as-measles-fight-stalls)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Ukraine destroys about 70 percent of Russia's fastest drones, Zelensky says, but missile gaps still cost lives.**

**What You Need to Know:** Ukraine's president told the BBC his forces now destroy about 70 percent of Russia's fastest drones, while a shortage of missile interceptors is still costing lives. European Union leaders left a budget summit without a deal, and Spanish voters go to the polls within days. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview:** BBC
In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky told the BBC at his central Kyiv office that delays in American anti-ballistic missiles are costing lives and that Washington is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks. He called it strange that President Donald Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Vladimir Putin, and said an aggressor and a killer cannot be a friend, likening that to saying one was friends with Adolf Hitler during the Second World War. Since a bruising Oval Office encounter with Trump in 2025, the BBC reported, Zelensky has been careful in how he handles the United States. Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate an end to the loss of life; the BBC reported they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position than with Kyiv's. The latest round, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress. Zelensky's description was that the more they know, the more problems, and he said talks are expected to resume in December. On Thursday Trump posted on Truth Social that, at his own summit with Putin in China last week, he had urged Russia to pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe and that he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was a strong possibility. The BBC reported that, from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial hardline negotiating positions on everything. Zelensky said it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the American envoys had announced, and the BBC reported the Kremlin appears to be resisting. The BBC said Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move and to bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end, and that Russian strikes are growing more frequent and more deadly, with the number of civilians being killed at an all-time high. Zelensky called for real helpful allies who can push Russia, and said that trying to be very neutral with the aggressor means supporting the victims and also the aggressor. The BBC said the United States argues it is neutral in the search for a deal that can hold. Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters he wants to stop the killing, that he could say Putin is not a friend, and that he wants to make a deal; he added that walking in and saying he does not like Putin would repeat the problem of two leaders who really hate each other, which he called the biggest problem for a settlement. In the meantime, the BBC reported, air alerts day and night are a draining feature of everyday life: Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities, and Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response. Zelensky said the military can now destroy about 70 percent of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving, but that there is a very, very big deficit of interceptors for ballistic missiles. He said the Americans were delaying deliveries of Patriot systems, that it is a pity they made a focus on the Middle East and help them more, and that the deficit of these missiles is people's lives.
Ranks: Ukrainians under Russian fire, and the governments in the talks · whether interceptors arrive and talks move · December, when Zelensky expects talks to resume Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820q9wgrpyyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)
Source: [bbc.com](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c820q9wgrpyyo)

**EU leaders split over budget spending and a $49 billion loan to Ukraine:** France 24
In the European Union, French President Emmanuel Macron set an end-of-year deadline for an agreement on the next seven-year budget after the continent's leaders ruled out any chance of a deal at their summit on Thursday, France 24 reported. That report framed the split as one over budget spending and a $49 billion loan to Ukraine. What did not close on Thursday, on that account, is both the multi-year spending plan and the loan. Yeni Safak reported the budget summit ended early, and that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said positions remain far apart. A separate report from tovima.com said the talks ended without agreement as divisions persist. Macron's deadline, as France 24 reported it, is the end of this year, after leaders themselves had already ruled Thursday out. The loan figure in the France 24 account is $49 billion, tied to Ukraine, and it sits inside the same unresolved argument as the seven-year budget.
Ranks: European Union governments and Ukraine's financing · a seven-year budget and a $49 billion loan left unsigned · end of this year, Macron's deadline Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261127-eu-leaders-split-over-budget-spending-and-a-49-billion-loan-to-ukraine)
Source: [en.yenisafak.com](https://en.yenisafak.com/world/eu-budget-summit-ends-early-as-merz-says-positions-remain-far-apart-3726058)
Source: [tovima.com](https://www.tovima.com/politics/eu-budget-talks-end-without-agreement-as-divisions-persist/)

**Spain general election 2026: Could Sánchez lose power?:** France 24
In Spain, voters head to the polls in just three days for a snap election after eight years of Socialist-led rule, France 24 reported. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is fighting to stay in power. France 24 said an alliance between the conservative People's Party and the far-right Vox could bring his time in office to an end, and framed the open questions as the key issues and what is at stake. The Globe and Mail dated the vote to November 29 and said Vox, which it described as an anti-immigrant faction, is promising economic restoration and conservative social values and stands to make gains. The New York Times named Santiago Abascal and reported that Spain's far-right era ended in 1975. The Times wrote that if the polls are right, Abascal's Vox could become the first far-right group to join a Spanish government since the days of Franco; that is the paper's conditional, not a result. France 24 did not publish a pollster, a sample, or a date range for any survey in the text available today. The ballots are still ahead of any count. What changes, if the alliance France 24 described takes office, is who governs after eight years of Socialist-led rule; what changes if it does not is that Sánchez remains. Neither outcome is known today.
Ranks: Spain's electorate · who forms the next government · November 29, the date The Globe and Mail gives Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261127-spain-general-election-2026-could-s%C3%A1nchez-lose-power)
Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-where-spains-far-right-vox-party-is-taking-hold-ahead-of-sundays/)
Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/27/world/europe/santiago-abascal-vox-spain-far-right.html)

**‘I cannot go to work’: Iranians contend with pollution as well as US war:** Al Jazeera
In Iran, the threat of American bombs is not the only danger residents of the capital must contend with, Al Jazeera reported: checking the air has become part of the daily routine. Tehran resident Ghoral, 40, told Al Jazeera that headaches, shortness of breath and blurred vision he once had only in the heavily polluted cold seasons are now year-round. He said the nausea hits even before the Meteorological Organization announces that the air is polluted, and that on heavily polluted days he tries to leave the house as little as possible, which means he sometimes cannot go to work, cutting his income, while the cost of a doctor and of medicine for his breathing problems rises. Hossein, 36, who both lives and works in the city centre, told Al Jazeera that for someone like him pollution is no longer just a part of life; it has become life itself. He said there is little anyone can do except escape the city as often as possible, particularly in winter, and that at the very least he tries to spend weekends in nearby cities where the air is better. Weather apps, Al Jazeera reported, are used less for rain or thunderstorms than for readings of fine particulate matter, PM2.5, the tiny airborne particles that can be deadly when breathed in over a prolonged period. The second half of the year has traditionally been a time of temperature inversion, when a layer of warm air traps cooler air and pollutants close to the ground and keeps them from dispersing. Pollution has become year-round, Al Jazeera reported, but it is particularly bad in winter, when that trapping is common, in cities and industrial areas. Mashhad, Isfahan, Shiraz, Tabriz and Ahvaz are also grappling with it. For more than half of the autumn and winter months, warnings are regular, advising people with heart and respiratory conditions to take precautions, and advising children, older people and pregnant women to stay indoors and avoid outdoor activities. The Meteorological Organization uses a yellow weather warning for days when pollution is particularly high; on those days schools typically cancel outdoor physical education. When levels approach an orange weather warning, generally an air quality index above 140 on a scale of 0 to 500, additional restrictions may follow: some employees switch to remote work, an odd-even licence-plate scheme limits cars, schools close, and some university classes move online. Dr Hadi Yazdani, who works at a medical centre in Isfahan, told Al Jazeera that one of the first signs of rising pollution is more hospital visits by patients with chronic asthma and other respiratory conditions. Figures from the Ministry of Health, as Al Jazeera reported them, say hospital visits for those conditions and for heart conditions rise by as much as 50 percent in winter, and that eye and skin problems also tend to become more common. Yazdani said children and older people are particularly vulnerable, that they may develop new illnesses or see existing ones worsen, and that because pollution reduces the circulation of fresh air, respiratory infections such as influenza and COVID also become more prevalent.
Ranks: Residents of Tehran and other major Iranian cities · lost work, higher medical costs, and winter hospital visits up as much as 50 percent · this winter, already under way Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/11/27/i-cannot-go-to-work-iranians-contend-with-pollution-as-well-as-us-war)

**Russia Moved Fuel by Train to a Secret Forest Depot—Ukraine Found and Destroyed the Supply Hub:** UNITED24 Media
In Ukraine, forces have destroyed a concealed Russian fuel and lubricants depot, along with supporting infrastructure, in the occupied Luhansk region, UNITED24 Media reported, targeting a logistics network that supplied Russian military units operating in Ukraine. The strikes targeted facilities in Vilkhove and Dovzhansk as part of Operation Hell-3, according to statements published on November 27 by Ukraine's 1st Azov Corps of the National Guard and the 9th Army Corps. Those statements said the operation was carried out jointly by the SxLüd unit and the Signum Unmanned Systems Battalion of Ukraine's 59th Assault Brigade. Russian troops belonging to the Center military grouping had established the fuel storage inside a forest, the statements said, using underground tanks to conceal its location and reduce its vulnerability to Ukrainian strikes. The Russian military also used camouflage, electronic warfare systems, and mobile firing teams intended to defend the hub against aerial attacks. Despite those precautions, Ukrainian units said they located and destroyed the concealed depot and the infrastructure supporting its operations. The facility served as a distribution point: fuel was transported to the depot by rail, then transferred into vehicles and delivered to individual Russian units. UNITED24 also reported earlier accounts that Russia's worsening fuel crisis was beginning to disrupt military operations in Ukraine, with Russian troops reporting reduced gasoline and diesel deliveries, strict refueling limits, and growing difficulty supplying frontline positions. In some cases, that reporting said, Russian troops are forced to abandon military equipment because it runs out of fuel. Recently, UNITED24 reported, Russian troops abandoned a working T-72 tank on the battlefield during a retreat after it simply ran out of fuel. The November 27 statements are Ukrainian military accounts of a strike already carried out; they are not a Russian confirmation.
Ranks: Russian units supplied from that Luhansk hub, by Ukraine's account · a concealed fuel point and its rail-to-vehicle chain · already struck, statements dated November 27 Source: [united24media.com](https://united24media.com/war-in-ukraine/russia-moved-fuel-by-train-to-a-secret-forest-depot-ukraine-found-and-destroyed-the-supply-hub-24769)

**India busts cyberfraud and trafficking network rescuing 164 foreigners:** BBC
Indian police say they broke a cyberfraud and trafficking network and rescued 164 foreigners lured by information-technology job promises and allegedly forced into cybercrime.
Ranks: 164 rescued foreigners · removal from alleged forced cybercrime · already carried out, police say Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crkgvjy7q83wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Thanksgiving storm on U.S. East Coast knocks out power, disrupts flights:** CBC
A Thanksgiving storm on the United States East Coast cut power to nearly 1 million customers at one point, with gusts up to 112 km/h.
Ranks: East Coast power customers, nearly 1 million at the peak · outages and disrupted flights · Thursday into the holiday weekend Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/u-s-thanksgiving-storm-power-flight-delays-9.7438358?cmp=rss)

**Australia sanctions suspects in Iran-linked anti-Semitic attacks:** Al Jazeera
Australia, Al Jazeera reported, sanctioned two men alleged to have planned antisemitic attacks for Iran's Revolutionary Guard, aiming to restrict their funds.
Ranks: Two sanctioned men, and the funding path alleged · funds restricted, not a court verdict · sanctions announced today Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/27/australia-sanctions-suspects-in-iran-linked-anti-semitic-attacks?traffic_source=rss)

**New Zealand PM says coalition negotiations could take time after election deadlock:** Xinhua
New Zealand's prime minister says coalition negotiations could take time after an election deadlock.
Ranks: New Zealand's next government · who can assemble a majority · talks under way, duration not set Source: [english.news.cn](https://english.news.cn/20261127/8812408540fc4b24b3d7f2f30c728d5b/c.html)

**Montgomery County certifies 2026 general election results:** Wiss Now
Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, certified the 2026 general election on a 2-0 vote, with turnout at 63.06 percent.
Ranks: Montgomery County's 396,211 voters who cast ballots · results now certified · certified Monday, the legal deadline Source: [wissnow.com](https://wissnow.com/news/montgomery-county-certifies-2026-general-election-results/)

### Both Sides: Should Washington stay neutral between Kyiv and Moscow?
The question is whether the United States should stay neutral between Ukraine and Russia while envoys seek a peace deal, or press Moscow as the aggressor. President Volodymyr Zelensky, speaking to the BBC in Kyiv, said that when you try to be very neutral with the aggressor you support the victims and you also support the aggressor, and that this is not right. His best reason is the cost in lives. He said delays in Patriot anti-ballistic missiles leave a very, very big deficit of interceptors, that the Americans have focused more on the Middle East, and that the deficit of these missiles is people's lives. He said Abu Dhabi talks earlier this month made no obvious progress — the more they know, the more problems — and he wants real helpful allies who can push Russia. He called a photo of Donald Trump embracing Vladimir Putin strange, and said an aggressor and a killer cannot be a friend. President Trump's case, given to reporters on Thursday, is that he wants to stop the killing and make a deal. He said he could say Putin is not a friend, but that walking in and saying he does not like him would repeat the problem of two leaders who really hate each other, which he called the biggest problem for a settlement. The BBC said the United States argues it is neutral so a settlement between the two sides can hold. Trump also wrote on Truth Social that, at a summit with Putin in China last week, he urged Russia to pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe, and he called a peace deal with Ukraine a strong possibility. Zelensky said talks are expected to resume in December. Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820q9wgrpyyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Five people died in occupied Zaporizhia as missiles struck Kyiv’s east side.**

**What You Need to Know:** Five people were killed in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia as Russian missiles struck the east side of Kyiv. U.S. regulators also cleared a plan for a million orbital data satellites, and an explosion and fire injured seven people at a Bangkok refinery. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia: Al Jazeera**
In Ukraine, a drone attack killed at least five people and wounded three in Vesioloye, in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia, Moscow-installed governor Yevgeny Balitsky wrote on Telegram on Thursday. He said the strike hit a parking lot. Russian forces hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles late on Wednesday. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the missiles struck a shopping centre and two other buildings on the east side of the Dnipro, and warnings to remain in shelters were still in place. Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said residents heard loud impact sounds and that those impacts injured at least seven people. She said people in frequently hit districts go to shelters even before sirens, and that Russia has heightened attacks on energy facilities as winter arrives. Russia’s Defence Ministry said, in an account carried by Interfax, that its forces carried out a massive overnight strike on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and struck a dry cargo vessel southeast of Odesa, which the ministry alleged was carrying military equipment and dual-use goods. The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said Ukrainian forces had earlier hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow and damaged five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs. Russian authorities reported repelling drone attacks in the Tuymazinsky district of Bashkortostan and in Nevinnomyssk, in Stavropol. Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia is pressing Kyiv’s military infrastructure, straining air defences and supply chains, and hitting power plants ahead of cold weather to wear down morale and inflict economic damage. MacAlpine said Ukraine’s energy capacity is below 40 percent of pre-war levels, with combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and the region repeatedly offline. Russia began its full-scale invasion in February 2022 and has claimed annexation of Zaporizhia, which it partially controls, since September 2022. Fighting has continued despite a renewed U.S.-backed push to end the war. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, answering Donald Trump’s description of Vladimir Putin as “my friend,” told CNN, “For us, he is a killer.”
Ranks: people in Kyiv and occupied Zaporizhia · at least five dead, with further wounded, and power already under 40 percent · immediate Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/ukraine-drone-attack-kills-five-in-russian-occupied-zaporizhia)
Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/ukraine-drone-attack-kills-five-in-russian-occupied-zaporizhia?traffic_source=rss)

**Trump, NATO chief caution Russia as attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure intensify: CNBC**
In the United States, President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte urged Russia, in a joint statement on Thursday, not to take any actions that would further expand the war in Ukraine. They met on Wednesday at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, called the meeting very impactful, and said Russia’s nearly five-year war and the Iran war were among the topics. Their statement said they discussed the importance of Russia avoiding actions that intentionally or unintentionally expand the war, and of obtaining a peaceful resolution as rapidly as possible. The Florida meeting followed Trump’s talks with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Asia, which raised concern among European lawmakers about Washington’s commitment to transatlantic security. At that meeting Trump described Putin as his friend. Rutte, a consensus builder during nearly 14 years as Dutch prime minister, has often used flattery with the U.S. president; Trump has called him a great leader and NATO’s biggest asset, while some have questioned whether that approach has delivered tangible benefits. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday accused the Kremlin of escalating threats toward European security, citing the Baltic region, Poland and the Black Sea, and said Russia knows what it wants and wants more than Ukraine. In Kryvyi Rih, Russian attacks disrupted power supplies and stopped municipal electric public transport, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the city’s defense council. Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday that strikes on the power sector damaged infrastructure and caused outages in five regions as cold weather set in. A spokesperson for Russia’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment on Thursday morning, and the Kremlin has repeatedly denied seeking military confrontation with NATO countries.
Ranks: Ukrainians under bombardment and NATO governments watching Washington · a joint warning, not a ceasefire · this week Source: [cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/26/trump-nato-rutte-russia-ukraine-war.html)

**Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved: BBC**
In the United States, the Federal Communications Commission has approved a SpaceX plan to launch a million satellites to process artificial-intelligence data in orbit, the first licence of its kind. The project, Starmind, would use sunlight to power the satellites and send results back to Earth. The commission said the project would support America’s booming super intelligence economy. Chairman Brendan Carr said it opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth, and that it can unite strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce economic leadership, and expand prosperity at home. Elon Musk wrote on X: “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” SpaceX says orbital data centres are the most cost- and energy-efficient way to meet demand for computing power beyond terrestrial capabilities. Opposition to data centres on Earth has grown, including in the United States, where experts say they were a factor in large Republican losses in the midterm elections. Amazon criticised the plan as a lofty ambition rather than a real plan. The American Astronomical Society said it was disheartened and dismayed, and that the constellation would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the public’s ability to study the night sky, because the satellites would be larger, brighter, more numerous, and visible as extremely bright objects for longer. Under the licence, deployment must begin no later than November 2033, with 10 percent deployed by November 2035 and 50 percent by November 2038. SpaceX has said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. The satellites would operate in low-Earth orbit between 500 and 2,000 kilometres, communicate with Starlink’s more than 10,000 satellites, and relay data to Earth. Professor Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the idea seemed technically feasible, but that whether it makes sense at scale still needs analysis, and that laser links from the ground are not yet perfected for the data volumes expected. It is unclear whether a million satellites will fly, or whether SpaceX sought room for more than it will use.
Ranks: astronomers, AI users, and people under those orbits · a licence for up to a million satellites · first launch sought next year; deployment deadlines from 2033 Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp836l8n1jgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)
Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/26/g-s1-155940/fcc-spacex-satellites-data-centers-in-space)

**Ships in Baltic and Mediterranean targeted by Ukraine and Russia: DW**
Ukraine has struck Russian ships far from its own coast, including the cargo vessel Sparta II off Finland and the corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel, allegedly carrying weapons, off Libya. The strikes came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland near an international military exercise. Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO’s eastern flank. DW reports that Moscow has already pressed countries that support Ukraine with military provocation, hybrid operations and sabotage, while Ukraine has targeted Russian military and economic sites beyond its borders. Since the summer, attacks by Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea, hitting Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships and vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey. Ukraine has also used aerial and maritime drones against military airfields, oil refineries including one in Omsk, and vessels in the eastern Black Sea. On the Baltic, Russia has only a narrow coast flanked by Finland and Estonia, and uses it to supply Kaliningrad and to export oil with its shadow fleet. Even before Sparta II, Ukraine had hit oil terminals near St. Petersburg, at Ust-Luga and Primorsk. The corvette, part of the Black Sea Fleet, could not return through Turkey’s blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, and had been escorting cargo ships in the Mediterranean; DW described that corvette as sunk. The attacks, DW writes, send a political message that Russian ships can no longer feel safe anywhere. Elisabeth Braw of the Atlantic Council told DW that Sparta II was not a random shadow vessel simply moving oil above the price cap, that it was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies, and that Ukraine is showing it knows where such ships are and can hit them in whatever waters they are in. Kyiv’s stated goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes. Military experts and politicians also see a signal of strength from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ahead of possible peace talks. Ukrainian special forces are also said to have struck Russian military facilities in Syria before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, and are reported to have supported Tuareg fighters in Mali against the Malian army and Russian mercenaries.
Ranks: crews and trade on the Baltic, Mediterranean and Black Sea · Russian ships hit far from Ukraine · already underway Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/russia-ukraine-war-extends-to-the-baltic-and-the-mediterranean/a-80054604)
Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/russia-ukraine-war-extends-to-the-baltic-and-the-mediterranean/a-80054604?maca=en-rss-en-world-4025-rdf)

**Seven injured in explosion at oil facility in Thailand’s Bangkok: Al Jazeera**
In Thailand, an explosion and fire at Bangchak Corporation’s Phra Khanong refinery in eastern Bangkok injured at least seven people, four of them seriously, Bangkok’s Erawan Emergency Medical Centre said. An earlier video report said no casualties had been reported, and that the blast could be felt for several kilometres, with authorities already urging nearby residents to evacuate. The company said it shut down all production units, contained the incident, and brought the situation under control. The Bangna District Office, on Facebook, urged people nearby to evacuate immediately and said the cause was under investigation. Videos showed flames high above the site and thick black smoke across the skyline. Tony Cheng, reporting for Al Jazeera from Chiang Mai, said the explosion was heard at about 3 p.m. local time, in an industrial area near warehouses and Bangkok’s main port, while highways and major routes remained open. He said the site serves Bangkok and a large part of central Thailand, and that most oil imports for this part of the country go there, so the damage is likely considerable even if its full extent is not yet known. A citywide phone alert said the fire was under control and urged people to avoid the area. Bangchak describes the site as a modern complex refinery with a maximum capacity of 120,000 barrels per day. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he was monitoring the situation, that it appeared under control, and that the fire did not appear to be in the main production area, without further detail. An explosion at the refinery in July 2012, then owned by Bangchak Petroleum, triggered a large fire and no reported injuries, and raised questions about a large facility in what is now a residential area.
Ranks: neighbors of the refinery and fuel users in central Thailand · seven injured and production shut · immediate Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/explosion-occurs-at-oil-facility-in-thailands-bangkok?traffic_source=rss)
Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/26/explosion-rocks-bangkok-oil-depot?traffic_source=rss)

Britain told 100,000 military reservists to prepare for war amid Russian threats, a first since the Cold War.

Britain’s net migration fell to the lowest since 1997, pandemic aside, after government curbs cut arrivals from outside Europe.

In the United States, Texas Republicans and the Justice Department agree a border barrier cannot be removed for decades.

### Progress Watch
After fears of a lead plume, the U.S. Army detonated nearly five tonnes of degraded lead azide at an ammunition plant in Iowa and called the controlled blast a huge success. Smoke rose shortly after 9 a.m. local time on Wednesday, and the Army said the risk was as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible. Plans to detonate the compound, stored about 20 years and made more sensitive by recrystallisation, had been paused several times after public outcry and legal challenges. No level of lead exposure is considered safe, and children and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said air monitors were detecting zero airborne lead. He wrote that the agency would stay radically transparent as laboratory results arrive over the next 24 to 48 hours, that the goal was to finish all sampling by Thursday, and that crews would remain for any remediation if needed. More than 1,000 post-detonation samples had already come from homes, parks, farms and drinking-water taps, with churches, schools and playgrounds due next. The Army said FEMA had issued an all-clear, and that surface-sampling results would be released once complete. President Donald Trump said reports showed mitigation efforts far exceeded expectations. Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson, watching from eight miles away and by camera at a home one mile from the site, said he felt relieved and neither felt nor saw anything. Sandy Mabeus, also eight miles out, closed windows, brought a cat inside, watched three live streams, and neither felt nor heard the blast. Farmer David Vandenberg, about 20 miles away, heard a rumble near nine o’clock after the Army Corps of Engineers sampled his yard and pond on Tuesday, and said he was happy the blast looked relatively contained. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said his state was seeing little to no impact and kept agencies on standby. Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg7l5ve251ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Two-hour daily power cuts begin Sunday for millions of Iranians as winter shortages bite.**

**What You Need to Know:** Two-hour daily power cuts begin Sunday for millions of Iranians as winter shortages bite. A split US verdict on Huawei, an unclassified breach at the C.I.A., and Taiwan's November 28 local elections follow that lead.
This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Iran rations electricity: How deeply are US sanctions, blockade biting?: Al Jazeera**
Iran is imposing rolling power cuts from Sunday, expected to last about two hours a day, on an electricity system that supplies 92 million people. President Masoud Pezeshkian asked millions of Iranians to conserve power in a televised interview with state broadcaster IRIB, conducted with the presidential-office chandeliers switched off and daylight let in. Tehran controls part of the world's largest natural gas field and has the world's third-largest proven oil reserves, yet government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani warned the gas shortfall could reach 430 million cubic metres a day this winter, compared with about 300 million in previous years. National Iranian Gas Company managing director Saeed Tavakoli said four processing plants damaged in the first phase of the conflict initially cut capacity by 230 million cubic metres, of which about 100 million had been restored, and the company warned that 11 of 31 provinces could face supply difficulties, particularly Mazandaran, Golestan and North Khorasan. Mohammad Allahdad, head of the national electricity company Tavanir, told state television that fuel conditions forced distribution restrictions from Sunday. An Al Jazeera analysis put usual generation at about 86 percent natural gas, roughly 7 percent oil-fired, about 5 percent hydropower and about 2 percent nuclear, mainly from Bushehr, Iran's only operational reactor. Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi said in August that war-related attacks had cost plants 4,200 megawatts, with repairs under way. Pezeshkian told ISNA that the attack on gas infrastructure had aggravated winter difficulties, and told investors on November 21, in remarks carried by IRNA, that Iran faces a "silent economic war" that is "tougher than a war with missiles," after February 28 strikes by the United States and Israel, later hits on energy sites, sanctions and months of a US naval blockade, with the war at an impasse.
Ranks: millions of Iranians on a grid serving 92 million · daily power and winter fuel cuts · from Sunday Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/25/iran-rations-electricity-how-deeply-are-us-sanctions-blockade-biting) Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/25/iran-rations-electricity-how-deeply-are-us-sanctions-blockade-biting?traffic_source=rss)

**How the War Turned Sudan Into a Country Without a Newspaper: Time Magazine**
Sudan has gone more than three years without a single newspaper printed, the first such gap in over a century, while the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces fight an information war and journalists are targeted. Thirty-four journalists have been killed in three and a half years, sixteen of them believed targeted for their work; hundreds have been displaced with their families and lost jobs, and dozens have been threatened, assaulted and detained. Most newspaper offices, television studios and radio stations have been looted, damaged or destroyed. Journalists have still tried to report costs Time put at more than 400,000 people estimated killed and 12 million believed displaced in a nation of 53 million. The war has split control, with the armed forces holding around 60 percent of the territory in the east and centre and the Rapid Support Forces about 40 percent, concentrated in Darfur and adjoining southern and western areas, and both sides tightly control what can be reported. The New York Times reported that the armed forces used banned chemical weapons, and a UN fact-finding report accused the Rapid Support Forces of sexual violence and slavery and described violence in El Fasher as bearing the "defining characteristics of genocide." On October 10, 2023, an Rapid Support Forces vehicle ran over and killed Halima Idris Salim, a Sudan Bukra correspondent, as she reported on a hospital in Omdurman. In December 2024 the armed forces arrested editor Yahya Hamad Fadlallah and his son in Khartoum; the Sudanese Journalists Syndicate and the Darfur Bar Association say he was falsely accused of collaborating with the Rapid Support Forces, tortured and denied diabetes treatment, then released on January 10, 2025, and died in hospital three days later. In May a Port Sudan court sentenced AlBalad TV journalist Rishan Oshi to a year in prison and a $16,553 fine for defamation after a Facebook post on government corruption. Syndicate chairman Abdelmonium Abouedries said, "The war came with a knockout punch to the press," and, "Truth became the war's first victim."
Ranks: a country of 53 million, plus killed, displaced and working journalists · information blackout inside a war already estimated to have killed more than 400,000 · already in force, with no printed paper for more than three years Source: [time.com](https://time.com/article/2026/11/25/sudan-war-rsf-elfasher-journalists-killed-arrested/)

**Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering: BBC World**
In the United States, a Brooklyn jury found Chinese telecommunications company Huawei guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and of bank fraud, and not guilty of racketeering, after a two-month trial. Jurors convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to violate US sanctions, and declined the racketeering count, which required a finding that the firm acted like a criminal enterprise. Federal prosecutors first announced the charges in 2019, after the late-2018 arrest in Canada of senior executive Meng Wanzhou, also known as Cathy Meng, who was held for three years and then released to China through a deal with US prosecutors. Assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand, including lying to banks about business in Iran and stealing technology from rivals. US Attorney General Todd Blanche said, "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft." Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis," and that it would take all necessary legal actions. Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said the company's reach — operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff — came from hard work, called the racketeering count a significant overreach the jury rejected, and said the defence had mixed emotions and had sought acquittals across the board. The Chinese government called the case US suppression of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests. Sentencing is planned for September 2027; Heberlig said Huawei will seek the lowest sentence and he fully expects an appeal.
Ranks: a firm with more than 200,000 staff and operations in 170 countries, plus US-China trade and sanctions enforcement · criminal convictions on 10 counts, with the enterprise charge rejected · sentencing in September 2027, appeal expected after that Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy49ngydqzpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Cyberattack exposes unclassified information from CIA system, US media reports: France 24**
In the United States, a cybersecurity breach at the C.I.A. and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence exposed some unclassified information, US media reported on Tuesday. The New York Times said the intrusions targeted an open-source intelligence analysis system that sifts public, unclassified material, which can still give analysts insight on its own or combined with classified spying. The Times, citing US officials and people familiar with the issues, said classified material was not jeopardised. A person familiar with the incident told the Associated Press, on condition of anonymity, that the issue that resulted in the breach has been resolved. The Times quoted an ODNI official as saying there had been no disruptions to critical capabilities, and said the C.I.A. declined comment. The report follows reported cyberattacks on the Agriculture Department and the F.B.I. Asked about the reported F.B.I. breach on Saturday, President Donald Trump told Fox News, "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," and said he had only recently learned of it. Last week an internal National Security Agency network used to communicate classified information was offline for a time, a nationwide ground stop snarled air travel after controllers struggled to reach pilots, and Apple, JPMorgan Chase and Microsoft had systems go down this month. White House cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross was fired last week. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday that the outages largely stem from a rush to patch and upgrade systems ahead of hackers using artificial intelligence tools at unprecedented scale.
Ranks: US intelligence agencies and users of travel, banking and everyday digital systems · unclassified material exposed, classified systems and travel already disrupted in the same wave · breach reported resolved; the wider outage pattern is current Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261125-cyberattack-exposes-unclassified-information-from-cia-system-us-media-reports)

**Fact check: Deepfakes and 'US abandons Taiwan' claims spread ahead of vote: DW World**
Taiwan holds local elections on November 28 that could shift power between the sovereignty-leaning Democratic Progressive Party and the Beijing-friendly Kuomintang, with consequences for ties among Taipei, Beijing and Washington. A month before the vote, AI-generated content featuring Democratic Progressive Party Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen spiked, and claims that the United States is abandoning Taiwan increased over the same period. DW Fact Check found identical headlines claiming US troops were withdrawing from Taiwan, repeated as articles and videos on the Chinese platforms NetEase and Sohu. The V-Dem Institute at the University of Gothenburg ranked Taiwan the country most severely targeted by foreign disinformation for eleven consecutive years, from 2014 to 2024. Taiwan's Ministry of the Interior has said foreign actors are increasingly interfering through election betting, invitations of Taiwanese citizens to China, donations and banquets, and temple and religious activities. An October 29 Facebook audio clip claims Shen admitted taking kickbacks on US arms purchases; multiple detection platforms flagged it as likely AI-generated, and the posting account was created that same day. A separate image claiming Shen was taking drugs carried an "AI content" label and was flagged by detector tools; Taiwanese outlet Watchout found that account had run at least five Facebook ads whose advertisers, Peng Zhiwei and Guo Yang, are based in China. Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence since 1949 despite Beijing's claim to the island as a province and repeated vows to annex it. Experts told DW that fake quotes and misleading clips are being used to weaken trust in US security commitments.
Ranks: Taiwan's voters, and the Taipei-Beijing-Washington relationship · false candidate and alliance claims in the final days before local elections · vote on November 28 Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-deepfakes-and-us-abandons-taiwan-claims-spread-ahead-of-vote/a-80004834?maca=en-rss-en-world-4025-rdf)

**3 Dead and Many More Trapped in Indonesian Mine After Heavy Rainfall: The New York Times World**
In Bogor, West Java, Indonesia, three people are dead and at least 23 workers are believed trapped in a flooded unauthorized gold mine.
Ranks: the trapped miners and their families · death and entrapment in a flooded shaft · since Monday, rescue under way Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/world/asia/indonesia-miners-trapped.html)

**Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours: BBC World**
In Colombia, police stormed a supermarket, freed around 20 shoppers and employees after 17 hours, and one gunman was killed.
Ranks: about 20 hostages and the store's community · a 17-hour ordeal ended by a police operation · already over Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp80mjr9emyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Surprise Eurostar strike cancels London, Paris and Brussels trains: France 24**
In France and Britain, a surprise Eurostar strike cancelled Paris-London trains on Wednesday, with delays also on some Belgium, Netherlands and Germany services, and refunds or rebooking offered.
Ranks: passengers on London, Paris, Brussels and connecting Eurostar routes · cancelled trains and delays today · Wednesday, with rebooking open now Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261125-surprise-eurostar-strike-cancels-london-paris-and-brussels-trains)

**UK Energy Bills Rise 26% as War Fuels Cost-of-Living Squeeze: Bloomberg**
In the United Kingdom, energy bills have risen 26 percent, with the war fueling a cost-of-living squeeze.
Ranks: UK households paying energy bills · a 26 percent rise · already in the bills Source: [bloomberg.com](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-25/uk-energy-bills-rise-26-with-war-fueling-cost-of-living-squeeze)

**Trump says US can sustain Iran war until end of January: TRT World**
President Donald Trump told the New York Post the United States is funded to continue the Iran war until the end of January.
Ranks: US forces, Iran, and a Congress that changes in January · a stated funding window for the war · through the end of January Source: [trtworld.com](https://www.trtworld.com/article/fe0faee829df)

### Both Sides: Should Israel strike Iran before a government is formed?
What is being decided is whether Israel strikes Iran before a coalition exists, ahead of an initial December 6 deadline to form a government. Interim Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu argues Israel needs a government free of what he calls the "taint" of Arab-party participation so it can answer what he says is an imminent military threat from Iran. On Tuesday, Defence Minister Israel Katz called for preemptive strikes before Iran could fully develop a chemical-weapons programme he said was already under way. Al Jazeera reported that US media said Netanyahu sent Mossad chief Roman Gofman to Washington in mid-November to urge joint strikes, citing intelligence that Tehran was developing chemical weapons, and that Gofman, Shin Bet chief David Zini, National Security Council chair Shmuel Ben Ezra and ambassador Yechiel Leiter back new strikes. In a November 19 Fox News interview, President Donald Trump said there was indication Iran was "looking at gases, looking at bio," because nuclear work had been shut down, while stopping short of committing to military action before the end of the year.

Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has told party members he has seen no imminent threat requiring action before a government is sworn in. Avigdor Liberman, who sits on the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee, told Israeli media, "If we end up seeing a strike right now, then we'll know that it's completely motivated by politics and not security concerns." Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir and researchers within Mossad reportedly see no case for an immediate attack, and defence officials have warned Netanyahu that new attacks could trigger a wider regional conflict.

Eisenkot's bloc has 48 seats, 13 short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He could look to Arab parties' 19 seats from outside government, which Netanyahu's supporters reject. Likud has 46 recommendations after United Torah Judaism endorsed neither candidate. Eisenkot has ruled out serving under Netanyahu and wants a unity government that shares leadership. Talks between his Yashar party and Likud ended without a deal. The next dated step is December 6. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/25/could-netanyahu-take-israel-into-another-war-with-iran-to-cling-to-power) Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/25/could-netanyahu-take-israel-into-another-war-with-iran-to-cling-to-power?traffic_source=rss)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Reports of a nuclear satellite launch within sixty days push Nato to vow space defence.**

**What You Need to Know:** German media reports of a possible Russian nuclear-armed satellite, shared among Nato countries this month, drew a pledge from the alliance to defend the space element of its territory. Separately, Gaza health officials warned of a meningitis surge as they reported new deaths from Israeli strikes, and Nvidia restored Jensen Huang after President Donald Trump said he had pressed the board. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports: BBC**
In Germany, Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the alliance will defend against threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite. Public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutscher Zeitung, citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, said a satellite dubbed Sputnik-S was equipped with a nuclear warhead and could disrupt or destroy other satellites, including communications and observation craft. France 24 reported that the accounts cited unnamed German military and BND sources and described a possible launch in the coming weeks; the BBC said intelligence reports of a launch in the next sixty days had been shared among Nato countries this month, and that it was not clear which country wrote them. Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports, called them not new yet no less shocking, and said they reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue, while government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said they were being taken very seriously and also warned against excessive nervousness over hypothetical dangers. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports and dismissed stories citing unknown sources as hardly worth taking seriously; the Russian embassy in Berlin rejected what it called unfounded allegations and a propaganda campaign. Beside Merz in Berlin, Rutte said Nato will defend every inch of its territory, including space, that the alliance has a variety of response options, and that it will assess deterrence and defence and update them where necessary. Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. European Space Agency head Josef Aschbacher called nuclear weapons in space the ultimate nightmare scenario, and Bleddyn Bowen of Durham University told the BBC a nuclear blast in space would have massive effects on more than 15,000 active satellites and would be indiscriminate enough to damage Russia's own space infrastructure. In 2024 the United States accused Russia of developing a space-based anti-satellite weapon with a nuclear warhead; Russia denied it, and President Vladimir Putin said then that Russia remained categorically against deploying nuclear weapons in space.
Ranks: militaries and societies that rely on shared satellites · a reported orbital nuclear weapon would threaten communications and observation craft · a claimed window of sixty days, not confirmed Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9x2er1ry2mzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)
Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261124-is-russia-preparing-to-launch-a-nuclear-armed-satellite)

**Israeli air strikes in Gaza kill 7 as doctors warn of meningitis outbreak: Al Jazeera**
In Gaza, health officials reported at least seven Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes, including a child and police officers, as the Ministry of Health issued an epidemic alert over meningitis. Dr Nidal Ghoneim, deputy director general of primary care, said cases rose to 272 in October, more than eight times a typical month of 30 to 50, and that 15 people have died of the disease since the start of this year, including five in August, September and October. He said bacterial meningitis, the most serious form, reached 108 cases in October, against a usual 10 to 20 a month, and that another 100 cases have been recorded since the start of November. The ministry warned that the spread threatens thousands of people, particularly children, given deteriorating health and environmental conditions. Medical sources said three Palestinians, including a child, were killed in a strike on the Wadi Gaza area in the centre of the Strip. The Palestinian news agency Wafa said an Israeli drone strike on al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, killed three and wounded five, and Al Jazeera's Hind Khoudary reported that those three were police officers. Wafa also said a person died of injuries after being targeted in Jabalia camp in northern Gaza, and that two civilians were killed Monday night in an air strike on Gaza City. Khoudary said dozens more were injured across the Strip and that strikes have continued daily even though a ceasefire was agreed.
Ranks: people in Gaza, especially children · deaths reported today and a meningitis rate far above the usual month · immediate Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/israeli-air-strikes-in-gaza-kill-7-as-doctors-warn-of-meningitis-outbreak?traffic_source=rss)

**Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang: BBC**
In the United States, Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over extramarital affairs, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy, after pressure from President Donald Trump. Trump said he made the deal with the board, which had rejected Huang's initial offer to return, and told CNBC the board asked for assurance on the national security threat and was given assurances based on everything officials know. He said it is a threat to lose Huang, not to have him, and when asked whether stock losses after the resignation influenced him, he said probably so. Huang resigned on 12 November; last Tuesday the board said it did not intend to reinstate him, and chairman Harvey Jones later said the return was in the best interests of stockholders, employees, partners and customers. The board said it had input from senior levels of the US government and was confident the reinstatement posed no national security risk. The BBC says the comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as the share price jumped 31 percent, lifting other tech shares and Asian markets while European markets were flat, though the price remains down over the past month amid wider concerns about the AI industry. Trump and Nvidia face backlash from lawmakers, and Huang is due before Congress next week over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China; China has denied the spying allegations. On Monday the Commerce Department said it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang, no relation, was chief executive. A BBC review of disclosures found Trump bought Nvidia shares worth between $23 million and $86 million over two years, including a $265,000 purchase and sales of as much as $15,000 in September, in 85 separate purchases; Huang, 63, co-founded the company in 1993.
Ranks: users of AI chips and US national-security oversight · the person who leads the central AI chipmaker is back, with a congressional hearing next · this week, hearing next week Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y1k8ez407o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**How the AI trade could trap even cautious investors: DW**
In Germany, asset manager Gerd Kommer told DW that a portfolio with 70 percent in one country, the United States, does not reasonably represent the global economy, which he said is more resilient than any national economy. He said investors need exposure to every sector and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio. DW reports that flagship index funds buy shares according to market value, so the larger a company grows, the more of it they hold, and that these funds hold pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index, which covers more than 2,400 firms in 47 markets, are US Big Tech names, and the other is TSMC, which produces 90 percent of high-end AI semiconductors. Those 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index, and nearly two-thirds of its value is in US-listed companies even though they are only about a fifth of its firms. In MSCI's Emerging Market index, the top 10 make up 37.5 percent of value, TSMC alone almost 16 percent, and tech, chip and internet firms are eight of the largest holdings, beside one Chinese bank and one Indian bank. Dimitri Vayanos of the London School of Economics told DW his model suggests flows into index funds have larger price effects when the large stocks are in the same industry, because optimistic buying is reinforced when funds add to winners. Economists told DW that investors looking for shelter from the AI trade are finding few places to go, partly because of how these indexes work.
Ranks: hundreds of millions of passive savers · their global funds are heavily tied to a few AI-linked firms · already the case in current indexes Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/how-the-ai-trade-could-trap-even-cautious-investors/a-80016412?maca=en-rss-en-world-4025-rdf)

**Quebec court rules MNAs must swear fealty to the King: The Globe and Mail**
In Canada, Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers ruled that members of the provincial legislature must take an oath of allegiance to King Charles III before they can assume their duties in the National Assembly. He granted an emergency application to suspend a 2022 law that had abolished the requirement to swear fealty to the British monarch. Demers wrote that, contrary to what it may seem, the oath plays a vital role in democracy. He added that the oath acknowledges the primacy of the Constitution, personified by the King. After the October 5 election, the province's 127 legislators swore allegiance only to the people of Quebec. The National Assembly is set to resume next week. The Globe and Mail reported the ruling in a decision released Tuesday.
Ranks: Quebec's 127 legislators and the voters they represent · they cannot sit without the royal oath the 2022 law had dropped · before the assembly resumes next week Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-politics-insider-quebec-court-rules-mnas-must-swear-fealty-to-the-king/)

**Malaysia set to return thousands of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar: Al Jazeera**
Malaysia is set to return thousands of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar, five days after the ICJ ruled Myanmar committed genocide against that minority.
Ranks: thousands of Rohingya refugees · forced return to Myanmar after a genocide ruling · announced, timing of returns not dated here Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/malaysia-set-to-return-thousands-of-rohingya-refugees-to-myanmar-2?traffic_source=rss)

The European Union has inked a trade deal with Indonesia to cut tariffs and catalyze investment, the Wall Street Journal reports.
Ranks: EU and Indonesian exporters and investors · tariffs are to be cut under a signed deal · as the agreement takes effect, date not given here Source: [wsj.com](https://www.wsj.com/economy/trade/eu-inks-trade-deal-with-indonesia-to-cut-tariffs-catalyze-investment-9810d41f)

Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is set Wednesday to be the first foreign astronaut on China's Tiangong station, carrying what he called the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.
Ranks: Pakistan's space programme and China's station partners · a first foreign crew member flies · Wednesday Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific/20261124-china-to-launch-first-space-mission-with-a-foreign-astronaut)

**Japan’s Leader, in Break with U.S., Defends International Criminal Court: The New York Times**
Japan's leader, Sanae Takaichi, welcomed the International Criminal Court's president and vowed to accelerate financial support despite a Trump administration effort to cripple the court.
Ranks: the International Criminal Court and states that fund it · Japan pledges faster money as Washington tries to weaken the court · announced, no payment date given Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/world/asia/japan-international-criminal-court-takaichi-trump.html)

**'Brexit means Brexit' no more? Why the U.K. now wants closer ties with the EU: CBC**
CBC reports Britain's Labour prime minister, Andy Burnham, has nudged open the door to closer ties with the European Union, a move some are already calling a Breturn.
Ranks: people in Britain and EU trade partners · a prime minister has opened talk of closer ties, not a treaty · no dated negotiation in the report Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/brexit-breturn-andy-burnham-uk-eu-ties-9.7433260?cmp=rss)

### Both Sides: Whether Nato should change space defence over Russian satellite reports
Nato is deciding how to treat German media reports, shared among allies this month, that Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite within sixty days. Secretary general Mark Rutte said the alliance will assess deterrence and defence and update them where necessary.

The case for treating the reports as a reason to harden space defence starts with Rutte: space is part of defending every inch of Nato territory, and he said the alliance has a variety of response options. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's strongest point is that the reports, which he neither confirmed nor denied, reveal an escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue, even if they are not new. Josef Aschbacher, head of the European Space Agency, called nuclear weapons in space the ultimate nightmare scenario. Bleddyn Bowen of Durham University gave the practical stake: more than 15,000 active satellites, and a blast would be indiscriminate.

The case against acting on the reports as if a launch were established starts with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov: he had not seen them, and stories citing unknown sources are hardly worth taking seriously. The Russian embassy in Berlin said the claims are unfounded allegations and part of a propaganda campaign. German spokesman Stefan Kornelius, while saying the reports were taken very seriously, warned against excessive nervousness over hypothetical dangers. Russia has signed the 1967 Outer Space Treaty banning weapons of mass destruction from orbit, and in 2024, after the United States accused Moscow of developing a nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon and Russia denied it, President Vladimir Putin said Russia was still categorically against nuclear weapons in space.

What happens next is the assessment Rutte described.
