# Omni View Top World News
> **Mary Peltola’s Alaska win gives Democrats a fifty-six to forty-four Senate edge.**

The same day, President Trump halted some sanctions on Russia and announced U.S. purchases of Russian diesel, British inflation rose to 3.6 percent, and a World Court genocide case on Myanmar moved toward a Thursday ruling. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Mary Peltola flips Alaska seat, giving Democrats a 56-44 edge in Senate: The Washington Post**
In the United States, the last unsettled Senate count of the midterms has now closed. The Washington Post reported that Mary Peltola flipped Alaska’s seat and that the win leaves Democrats with a 56-44 edge in the Senate. MS NOW reported that she unseated Senator Dan Sullivan, so the seat changes hands rather than staying with the incumbent the network named. The BBC reported that confirmation of her victory arrived two weeks after midterm counting began. The BBC said that confirmation caps what it called the party’s rout of the Republicans in the midterm Senate election. Those accounts describe a finished count, not a projection and not a forecast of any later contest. The balance those outlets state is fifty-six Democratic seats to forty-four on the other side, a margin that sets the chamber Democrats will organize. For Alaskans, the person who will hold the state’s Senate seat has changed; for the rest of the country, the reported change is which party holds the majority and by how many seats. No outlet in today’s file predicted a later race from this result.
Ranks: the U.S. Senate’s party balance · Democrats hold a 56-44 edge · confirmed after two weeks of counting Source: [washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/17/alaska-senate-election-live-results-mary-peltola-defeats-dan-sullivan/) · [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqev3v2ygzlvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) · [ms.now](https://www.ms.now/news/peltola-sullivan-alaska-senate-election-results)

**Putin Will Continue Ukraine War Despite Plans to Meet Trump, Intelligence Says: The New York Times**
In the United States, a policy shift on Russia landed on the same day President Donald Trump is due to talk about Ukraine with the leaders of Russia and China. The New York Times reported that he has halted some sanctions on Russia and announced that the United States will buy Russian diesel. The same account said intelligence judges that President Vladimir Putin will continue the Ukraine war despite plans to meet Trump. The sanctions step, as the Times stated it, is a halt to some measures, not a claim that every sanction has been lifted. The diesel announcement is a purchase by the United States, named as Russian diesel, not a general description of world oil trade. Ukraine is the subject the Times said Trump plans to raise with those two leaders. For Ukrainians, the reported American moves are fewer sanctions on Russia and a U.S. buyer for Russian diesel, while the intelligence judgment in the headline is that the war does not stop because a meeting is planned. The Times placed that judgment beside the sanctions halt and the diesel announcement as the facts of the day, not as a prediction of what the leaders will sign.
Ranks: Ukraine’s war and U.S.-Russia energy trade · some sanctions halted and diesel purchases announced; war assessed as continuing · now, with talks planned Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/politics/trump-putin-ukraine-war.html)

**UK inflation rises to 3.6% after petrol and diesel prices hit record high: The Guardian**
In the United Kingdom, the Office for National Statistics said consumer-price inflation rose to 3.6 percent in October, from 3.5 percent in September, matching City economists’ forecasts and the highest headline rate in a year. Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said fuel prices were once again a major contributor, and that annual costs of raw materials and of goods leaving factories are still climbing, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices. Petrol rose 5.2 pence a litre between September and October, to 174.7 pence, the highest in four years. Diesel rose 7 pence a litre, to 199.5 pence, the highest price on records dating to 1996. Motor fuel prices rose at an annual rate of 33.2 percent, the largest increase since July 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Guardian linked the October rise to fallout from the war in the Middle East. A Bank of England spokesperson said that conflict has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and that inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year because of cost pressures already in the pipeline. The Bank said it raised bank rate from 3.75 percent to 4 percent two weeks ago to limit how far higher energy costs pass into other prices, and that it will keep setting rates so inflation returns to the 2 percent target and stays there. Forecasters cited in the account look for a peak close to 5 percent next year. Markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year, and analysts said a rise could come as early as next month. Andy Burnham’s government has pledged household support. At last month’s budget, Chancellor John Healey announced a £100 winter handout for 20 million households. The October figures already include a 4 percent rise in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October. Cornwall Insight on Wednesday forecast a 26 percent jump in Great Britain energy bills from January, to £2,166 a year for a typical household. Core inflation was unchanged at 2.8 percent. Services inflation held at 3.7 percent, slightly under a City prediction of 3.8 percent. Food prices rose 0.9 percent, the slowest rate since September 2021, down from 1.3 percent in September. Air fares rose 1.8 percent between September and October on higher long-haul tickets, partly offset by cheaper European flights. Alcohol and tobacco prices rose 4.5 percent, influenced by the timing of a tobacco-duty increase at the start of the month.
Ranks: households across Britain · inflation at 3.6 percent, diesel at a record, bills forecast higher · October figures now, January bills forecast Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/18/uk-inflation-rises-energy-prices-iran-war-oil)

**Fears grow over US sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling: The Guardian**
At the International Court of Justice, a genocide case brought over Myanmar is due for a ruling the Guardian described as set for Thursday, and lawyers and diplomats are already arguing about what a finding would mean. The Guardian reported growing fears that the United States could sanction judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court finds that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide. The definition the court must apply is acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, and proving that intent has been the hard point in earlier cases. Myanmar denies genocide and says its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents. Lawyers for Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017. Judges have taken advice on how to protect their assets from possible U.S. sanctions, on the view that a genocide ruling could be read in Washington as lowering the legal threshold. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, described as close to the White House, has predicted that a genocide ruling will lead the United States to sanction the ICJ. The Guardian reported that the United States and Israel fear a final judgment may clarify how intent is established and so make it more likely the court later finds that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. The Gambia, as a litigant, appointed Pillay as an ad hoc judge; she is required to act as a jurist, not as an advocate for The Gambia. Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, told Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges that Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponize the law against our troops,” and asserted that Pillay is tipping the scales to lower the threshold so it can later be used against American and allied soldiers “whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.” He said Washington sees her agenda and will watch the proceedings closely. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Friday that for “this global elite,” international law is an instrument to advance their interests “under the pretence of universal principles,” and he warned the International Criminal Court against quoting laws to “men with swords.” The United States has already sanctioned ICC judges after arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and has sanctioned the ICC as an institution it called a rogue court, citing fear the court could pursue U.S. troops. A 24-page submission by the United Kingdom and five other mainly European states argued that intent should be judged from a range of facts and circumstances, assessed comprehensively and holistically. Israel has criticised adverse ICJ advisory opinions and refused to implement 2024 orders to admit more aid into Gaza and to cooperate with Unrwa.
Ranks: Rohingya survivors and later genocide cases · a possible first state genocide finding, with U.S. sanction threats on judges · ruling described for Thursday Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/us-sanctions-icj-judges-myanmar-genocide-ruling-israel-gaza-court)

**Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction: Al Jazeera**
In Sudan, a war that began in Khartoum in April 2023 has killed at least 59,000 people and forced 14 million from their homes in a country of 52 million, Al Jazeera reported. The fight is between the Sudanese armed forces and the Rapid Support Forces, former military allies, and the capital was an early centre of that struggle. Thousands in Khartoum State were trapped at home for weeks or forced to flee. The armed forces expelled the RSF from the region in May last year, and the capital has since become a haven for people leaving fighting elsewhere. Mohammed Awad was 17 when the war started. He told Al Jazeera he was pushed out of school and moved from state to state with his cousins looking for safety, and that he began taking drugs to forget what he saw in the first months, including friends and a cousin killed in front of him. He said he has entered rehabilitation centres many times, returned to addiction, takes pills and sometimes weed, and keeps failing when he tries to stop, though he wants to return to education. Government officials say insecurity and poverty have spread drug manufacturing and trade, particularly the amphetamine Captagon, and that areas now or formerly under RSF control are a particular problem. Lubna Ali, director of the Qadreen Center for Addiction Treatment, one of the few charitable centres dealing with the problem in Khartoum, said the centre kept providing medical care through the war and has seen a significant increase in people seeking treatment. Since the war broke out, the centre has treated 10,100 cases, from psychological support for war trauma to drug addiction, and Ali said 135 people have been treated in their recovery journey. Doctors in the capital told Al Jazeera demand for those services is growing. Young people, the report said, are especially exposed: violence, displacement, dead friends and relatives, interrupted school, and falling work. Weakened institutions and a worse security situation have undercut oversight and the health service’s ability to answer the addiction crisis.
Ranks: civilians in Sudan, including people seeking addiction care · at least 59,000 killed and 14 million displaced; treatment demand up · ongoing since April 2023 Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/18/traumas-of-sudan-war-is-seeing-a-wave-of-drug-addiction)

**EU proposes new €45 billion Ukraine loan to be repaid by Russia: France 24**
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed a 45-billion-euro Ukraine loan for 2027, about two-thirds of Kyiv’s needs, repaid from future Russian reparations.
Ranks: Ukraine’s 2027 finances · a proposed loan for about two-thirds of needs · announced Wednesday, still a proposal Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261118-eu-proposes-new-%E2%82%AC45-billion-ukraine-loan-to-be-repaid-by-russia)

**US loses measles-free status as cases soar: France 24**
The United States lost measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization said Tuesday, and Bolivia and Mexico lost theirs.

Ranks: Ukraine and its backers · allied rejection of U.S. criticism of deep strikes · ahead of the summit Source: [cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/ukraine-russia-war-trump-putin-deep-strikes.html)

### Both Sides: Ukraine’s deep strikes inside Russia
At a gathering of Ukraine’s allies in Brussels on Tuesday, the question was whether Ukraine should keep striking deep inside Russia, and whether its backers should keep enabling those strikes. France 24 reported that Elbridge Colby, a top U.S. defence official, criticised Ukraine’s “deep strikes” against Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky, at the same moment in the diplomatic calendar, urged Kyiv’s backers to send air defences without delay. The case against the deep strikes, as Colby put it by criticising them, is that the American official does not want that tactic to stand as the allies’ line. France 24 did not quote a longer military rationale from him. The case for pressing on, in the form France 24 reported, is the flat rejection from Germany and the United Kingdom, who hit back at the Americans’ suggestion. Their strongest stated position in that account is refusal: they did not accept the U.S. criticism. Zelensky’s request for air defences without delay is the Ukrainian government’s accompanying ask — protection at home while the argument over strikes inside Russia is unresolved. CNBC reported the same split as allies rejecting U.S. criticism of deep strikes ahead of a Trump-Putin-Xi summit. The next dated setting for the wider war talks is that summit, which other reporting placed on Thursday in Shenzhen, where President Trump has said the talks would cover the wars in Iran and Ukraine as well as nuclear disarmament. Nothing in today’s accounts records a vote that ends the strikes or a shipment that fills Zelensky’s air-defence request. # Omni View Top World News
> **Photos suggest a 227-metre Kerch span has fallen, shutting Crimea's road link.**

**What You Need to Know:** Photos suggest a 227-metre span of the Kerch bridge has fallen into the strait, and officials say the road link to occupied Crimea is shut, though Moscow says repairs will leave it better than before. Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian drones that Tehran says hit a US radar; President Trump reached Manila as ASEAN was closing; and five European governments set out a Rwanda hub for rejected asylum seekers. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Ukraine critically damages Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia: The Guardian**
Ukraine says it critically damaged the Kerch bridge, the road and rail link between Russia and Russian-occupied Crimea, in an overnight missile attack that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called an unprecedented operation and a response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure. The BBC reported that Ukraine says the attack took weeks to plan, while the Kremlin vows to rebuild. Zelenskyy wrote that Ukrainian forces had gradually destroyed air defences, radars and electronic-warfare equipment on the way to the bridge, that Palianytsia drones hit the road section, and that Neptune and other missiles hit the rail section; the Guardian said footage showed a Flamingo cruise missile seconds before impact, after a Monday strike on a central arch. Photos described by the Guardian suggest a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch Strait, which joins the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, and that the adjacent railway arch is also damaged. Ukrainian commentators told the Guardian the steel arch cannot easily be replaced, and that traffic can now leave the peninsula only by a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, exposed to Ukrainian drones. The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, said the bridge is no longer usable, that traffic is suspended, and that residents and visitors should not travel toward it. Russian officials quoted by Reuters insisted the damage was only minor and would be quick to repair; Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram that designers and builders are already gathered and that logistics are being sorted with regional leaders. After an emergency government meeting, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Khusnullin had briefed President Vladimir Putin, and told Izvestia the bridge would be restored and would be even better than before. The bridge was built eight years ago after the 2014 annexation, which Ukraine calls illegal; Ukraine struck it with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone in 2023. The Guardian said debris appears to have blocked the main navigable channel, 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep, used by ships from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol, and that the Rybar channel, which has close links to the defence ministry, warned that fitting a new arch would be formidable because Ukraine can now strike repair crews. Russian forces struck two major bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv late on Monday, plus other critical infrastructure, in drone and missile attacks.
Ranks: Forces and civilians who use the Crimea link, and Ukraine's effort to cut that route · a pictured span is down and traffic is suspended, with repair disputed · immediately Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/17/ukraine-strikes-critical-damage-russia-kerch-bridge-crimea)
Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/17/europe-ukraine-russia-crimea-kerch-bridge-attack-latest-news-updates)
Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw772jk4rvmxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Bahrain thwarts drone attack; Iran claims targeting US radar: Al Jazeera**
Bahrain said on Tuesday that its air defences intercepted a drone attack after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had struck a United States radar at the Sheikh Isa base, also referred to as the Isa airbase, in Bahrain, home of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. Blasts were heard over Manama after a phone alert warned of a potential threat and told people to go to the nearest safe place; the Interior Ministry later sent an all-clear, said precautionary measures remain, and urged caution. The Globe and Mail reported no casualties or damage from Tuesday's interception. The IRGC, in a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster IRIB, said the attack was part of efforts to counter hostile US activity in the region. Al Jazeera's Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, said that since Friday a pattern has emerged of Iran trying to restore deterrence, and that Tehran is tying this strike to what it calls continued violations of Iranian airspace rather than to one specific US attack. On Sunday the IRGC said it launched six drones at a US air-defence radar at Bahrain's Riffa airbase, which the Globe and Mail rendered as Al-Rifaa, after what it called hostile US actions; Bahrain said it had also intercepted several Iranian attacks that day. On Friday the IRGC claimed a hit on a US early-warning radar in Bahrain; the US military denied the facility was hit and said it intercepted two Iranian drones with no damage or casualties. These strikes come in a war that began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28 and that reports describe as stalled. President Donald Trump has said he might hold off attacking Iran if the United States does not face what he called provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, while keeping a US naval blockade over Tehran's disruption of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of global energy supplies before the war. On Tuesday Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi was in Oman, which has mediated; Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and he discussed safeguarding maritime corridors, the flow of shipping, and reviving talks to prevent escalation, the Omani foreign ministry said. Last week Iran attacked ship navigation systems on the Omani island of Didamar, in the strait. Tuesday's attack followed Bahrain's sentencing of 64 people, mostly Shiite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state, including Sheikh Isa Qassim, described by the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy as the spiritual leader of Bahrain's Shiite community, who has lived in Iran since 2018. Iran's foreign ministry condemned the ruling and called the accusations baseless. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned Iranian strikes in Bahrain in a call on Monday with Bahrain's foreign minister.
Ranks: People in Bahrain, US forces at the Fifth Fleet, and shipping through Hormuz · an intercepted strike and fresh talks, with no reported casualties Tuesday · today, inside a war that began in February Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/17/bahrain-thwarts-drone-attack-iran-claims-targeting-us-military-radar)
Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-iran-attacks-us-military-radar-system-in-bahrain-with-drones/)

**Trump arrives in Philippines for ASEAN Summit, will meet Quad leaders: The Tribune**
President Donald Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday on a 48-hour Asia trip, arriving as the 49th ASEAN summit was already wrapping up, the new step in a visit whose later meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin had already been expected. The New York Times reported he is due to meet President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and that, after less than 24 hours in Manila, he heads to the APEC summit in Shenzhen; The Tribune reported a state visit and lunch with Marcos on Wednesday, then departure for Shenzhen, with meetings on Thursday with President Xi and President Putin expected to cover Iran and nuclear non-proliferation. Soon after arrival he met leaders of the Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — the first in-person Quad leaders' summit in two years, according to the White House itinerary cited by The Tribune; Prime Minister Narendra Modi also took part in the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit in Manila. The Times reported that Southeast Asian leaders, tariffed even when they are allies, have come to see Washington as an unreliable partner and will look for any sign that the Republican midterm defeat has changed Mr Trump's approach, and that Quad partners are dealing with high energy prices after the Iran war, which the Times said he launched in late February without discussing it with them. In Shenzhen, the heart of China's robotics and artificial-intelligence industries, he needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets. It would be his third meeting with Mr Xi this year, and a three-way meeting with Mr Xi and Mr Putin would be the first of its kind. Before leaving Washington he told reporters they would talk about denuclearization, which he called a tough subject because it is very hard for any of them to say they will get rid of their nuclear weapons; Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one. He also said they would talk about Iran a little and that the situation was in very good shape; analysts told the Times that progress on Iran is unlikely, with Russia content to see energy prices elevated since the war began and China eager to see them fall. Thousands of demonstrators gathered in downtown Manila against his visit and against Pax Silica, a US-led effort to unite partners around artificial-intelligence supply chains independent of China; the Times reported that most were students who said their government was more focused on its relationship with the United States than on helping Filipinos. Russian state news agencies, citing the Kremlin spokesman, said Mr Putin could meet Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for APEC; it was not clear whether Mr Kim would attend. The Tribune reported that during the Philippines stop Mr Trump is also scheduled to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, and that the Philippines' ASEAN chairmanship has stressed maritime security and a code of conduct with China for the South China Sea.
Ranks: Governments across Southeast Asia and the US, Chinese and Russian tracks · meetings are underway, with no agreement announced today · over the next two days Source: [tribuneindia.com](https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/world/trump-arrives-in-philippines-for-asean-summit-will-meet-quad-leaders/)
Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/17/world/trump-asean-summit/heres-the-latest)
Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/world/asia/trump-manila-asean-late.html)
Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/world/asia/philippines-protest-trump-marcos.html)
Source: [hindustantimes.com](https://www.hindustantimes.com/videos/watch-pm-modi-joins-world-leaders-at-the-23rd-asean-india-summit-in-manila-shorts-101794911803028.html)

**5 European countries aim to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda: France 24**
Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced on Monday that they aim to set up a return hub in Rwanda where rejected asylum seekers could be sent from next year. The five, which have spearheaded talks with countries outside the European Union, said they also hope the move will deter more people from coming. France 24 reported that the plan drew immediate criticism from human rights groups. Al Jazeera reported that Rwanda is again being proposed as a return hub and that critics warn of potential human rights abuses.
Ranks: Rejected asylum seekers in five European countries, and Rwanda as the proposed destination · a transfer plan for next year, not yet in operation · announced Monday, aimed at next year Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261117-5-european-countries-aim-to-send-rejected-asylum-seekers-to-rwanda)
Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/17/why-are-five-eu-countries-reviving-plans-to-deport-migrants-to-rwanda?traffic_source=rss)

**Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank: The Guardian**
Britain's foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced the first sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build settlements in the occupied West Bank, which the Foreign Office calls illegal. The Guardian reported that the move is designed to hinder further building after, the Foreign Office said, Israel has refused to clamp down on settlements. He also placed sanctions on a right-wing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month. The package follows a pledge he made in September to respond to the expansion of settlements, which the Guardian said has been marked by rising violence against Palestinians. Miliband has argued that plans for the E1 development in the West Bank would make a two-state solution unviable. He has said he is trying to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.
Ranks: Israeli firms targeted for settlement plans, and Palestinians in the West Bank · a first set of UK company sanctions, meant to slow building · announced today Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/17/ed-miliband-israel-west-bank-settlements-sanctions)

**U.S. to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump visits Asia: The Globe and Mail**
The United States is restricting advanced-chip shipments to Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, routes Chinese firms have used to reach computing power for training artificial-intelligence models.
Ranks: Chinese AI developers and chip trade through three Southeast Asian countries · access to advanced chips and their computing power is being curbed · as the rules apply, during this Asia trip Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/international-business/asia-pacific-business/article-us-to-curb-chinas-access-to-ai-chips-as-trump-visits-asia/)
Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwq6e2qgvmlgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Russia says French troops in Ukraine show 'direct participation' in war, issues warning to Paris: France 24**
In Moscow, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said French troops in Ukraine are direct participation in the war, and that a message had gone to Paris.
Ranks: France, Ukraine and Russia's reading of outside military help · a participation claim and a warning, not a new battle · stated today Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261117-live-russian-attacks-target-bridges-in-kyiv-knocking-out-heating-and-water-ukraine)

**Congo Ebola Outbreak: How Fear and Mistrust Drive Community Spread: The New York Times**
In eastern Congo, health teams are struggling to slow Ebola as people delay care and treat sick relatives at home.
Ranks: People living with the eastern Congo outbreak · fatal delays and home care continue to spread infection · ongoing Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/world/africa/congo-ebola-community-transmission.html)

**Nations urged to exit fossil fuels as Turkey touts oil find: Winnipeg Sun**
At COP31 in Turkey, UN chief Antonio Guterres urged nations to plan a future without fossil fuels, while the host celebrated new oil reserves.
Ranks: Governments at the Turkey climate summit · a call to leave fossil fuels, set against a new oil find · stated today Source: [winnipegsun.com](https://www.winnipegsun.com/news/world/leaders-protesters-greet-trump-at-philippines-summit/article_dfe1627d-e5f8-54da-a182-03e33f00f4b6.html)

### Both Sides: Should Britain adopt Alan Milburn's youth plan?
Britain is arguing over a review by Alan Milburn on young people outside work, training or education. The Guardian reported that the full report has not formally been published, though it has circulated in Westminster on an embargoed basis since yesterday, so the parties already know its contents. No publication hour beyond that pending release is set out in today's account.

Milburn's case, as the Guardian led it, is that his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, while overall savings will take years. The reason offered for moving now is the scale of the problem already on the books. In the opposition responses the Guardian published, one argument said nearly a million young people are out of work or training, more than there are job vacancies in the entire country, and that a target to halve the number of Neets by 2036 needs growth, including what that response called scrapping Labour's jobs tax and joining the EU single market.

The Conservative case against, from Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, starts from the young people already on welfare. She said Conservatives agree with Milburn on the problem and want the review to succeed, and will back him where he takes up their proposals, including a shift from cash sickness benefits to support for milder conditions and a cut in national insurance for young people. She said he is right to criticise tax and regulation burdens Labour has put on business, but that the review is too cautious about reversing that damage, too often answers with a large and expensive state, fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in spending, and will not change anything for young people stuck on welfare now because nothing will happen for at least three years.

The Green party put the opposite objection. It said its alternative is proper work and training for proper pay, so young people can reach their potential without the threat of poverty and homelessness. Around that line, the published Green response rejected threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, and unsuitable short-term work, and treated the review as more of a model it says Andy Burnham had promised to end.

What happens next is formal publication of the review. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/live/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-youth-unempolyment-neets-economy-welfare-brexit-latest-news-updates)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Nearly 330,000 people are displaced as Yemeni forces leave the Red Sea strait to defend Aden.**

**What You Need to Know:** Nearly 330,000 people are displaced as Yemeni forces leave the Red Sea strait to defend Aden. A US official says a third American carrier has reached the Middle East, US liquefied natural gas flows hit a record, and South African police are investigating 17 deaths in two Sunday-night shootings. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Yemeni forces retreat to defend Aden from Houthis: BBC World**
In Yemen, Saudi-backed pro-government forces say they are moving troops off the Bab al-Mandab Strait to defend the interim capital, Aden, after weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement. The Southern Armed Forces said on Sunday they were withdrawing from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area to strengthen front lines, and said this step was driven by the priority of securing Aden and neighbouring governorates. Houthi-run media say the movement has taken control of the evacuated territory; Saudi Arabia has not commented. The pullback ends a weeks-long offensive near the shipping route the Houthis seized in a surprise offensive in September. Pro-government forces said they had secured the strait in early October, while the Houthis said they had captured Perim Island and the port city of Mokha a month before that claim. The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping through the waterway but would keep targeting vessels from Saudi Arabia, and the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and noted that since fighting escalated in August more than 60 percent of documented civilian casualties were women and children. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Aden, including an assault on 15 October on the presidential palace that killed five and injured 16; Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, and the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi cities and infrastructure. The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced as the fighting escalated, and hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Yemen's civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa; a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015, and a four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia.
Ranks: hundreds of thousands of displaced Yemenis, plus oil buyers · lost ground on a key strait and more risk to civilians · immediate Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg2xgyvnjpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?: Al Jazeera**
In the Middle East, a US official told Al Jazeera that the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived on Monday, the third American carrier in the region, joining the USS George Washington and the USS George H.W. Bush in the US Central Command area. The Pentagon and Central Command have not formally confirmed the arrival. Another official told Al Jazeera the ship reached the Middle East on 15 November after leaving San Diego in September. The United States and Iran agreed a two-week ceasefire in April and a broader memorandum of understanding in June that collapsed in early July. Mediators from Pakistan and Qatar have since tried to prevent a return to the full-scale attacks that hit the wider Gulf in March. Diplomatic efforts to permanently stop the US-Israel war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled. Last week President Donald Trump said further military strikes against Iran were "quite unlikely" and that the military component of the war was "effectively over" after talks with Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, while adding that the US military remains "locked and loaded" if conditions change. The Roosevelt, commissioned in 1986, carries more than 5,000 personnel and more than 60 aircraft, including F-18s, the US Navy says. A US official told Al Jazeera last month that the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, carrying more than 2,000 Marines, had also headed for the region; the Wall Street Journal reported those naval deployments could involve an additional 9,000 to 10,000 US soldiers in total, which the US military has not confirmed.
Ranks: Gulf states and shipping that depend on Hormuz · a third carrier on station while talks stay stalled · immediate Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/uss-roosevelt-arrives-in-middle-east-is-the-us-iran-war-about-to-resume?traffic_source=rss) · [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/uss-roosevelt-arrives-in-middle-east-is-the-us-iran-war-about-to-resume)

**Record US LNG Exports May Bring Relief to War-Strained Markets: Energy Connects**
In the United States, estimated pipeline deliveries to all US liquefied natural gas export plants climbed to about 21.8 billion cubic feet on Saturday. BloombergNEF data, reported by Bloomberg, put that flow at an all-time high and more than 12 percent above a year earlier. Pipeline gas to the Golden Pass project reached a record on Saturday, and flows to Sabine Pass were the highest since April. Bloomberg reported that the added supply could ease gas markets in Europe and Asia as the Northern Hemisphere enters winter. The war in the Middle East has forced countries to look elsewhere for cargoes and pushed prices to the highest in years. Prices in Asia, home to the largest importers, have tripled compared with pre-war levels, while European gas futures have climbed nearly threefold. US LNG output is poised to double by the end of the decade, and the International Energy Agency says an expected shift into oversupply has been pushed back at least two years by disruptions to output from the Persian Gulf.
Ranks: gas buyers in Europe and Asia · record US supply against prices still far above pre-war · this winter Source: [energyconnects.com](https://www.energyconnects.com/news/gas-lng/2026/november/record-us-lng-exports-may-bring-relief-to-war-strained-markets/)

**Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 17 dead: BBC World**
In South Africa, police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two shootings on Sunday night that they say are unrelated. Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus outside Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal; police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said officers found a white seven-seater riddled with bullet holes, and that the motive and the suspects' identities had not been established. Hours later, police found six men and three women shot dead inside a four-room shack in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, between 22:00 and 23:00, with bodies scattered across the rooms and spent cartridges outside. Brigadier Brenda Muridili said the Gauteng provincial commissioner had mobilised crime intelligence and a tracking team. Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder. The country is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang killings, and has one of the world's highest murder rates. In September, 18 people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg on 25 September, with 14 others injured, and the next day 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue near Cape Town, with 11 injured. Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining. In February President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development," and earlier this year the military was deployed with police in five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng. In January, five men were shot dead outside a shop in that Pretoria area in daylight.
Ranks: the families of 17 people, and communities in two provinces · two new mass killings where murder is already among the world's highest · immediate Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8y5x3n4kywpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**EU clears UniCredit takeover of Germany's Commerzbank: Yahoo Finance UK**
In Europe, the European Commission on Monday approved Italian bank UniCredit's takeover of Germany's Commerzbank. EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said Europe needs stronger banks that can compete, grow and support businesses and families, and that cross-border mergers can help banks operate more efficiently and better withstand economic shocks. The Commission approved the acquisition after finding the deal would not raise competition concerns. Ribera said the decision shows it is possible to support a stronger European banking sector while safeguarding competition and choice. The European Central Bank had already approved UniCredit's hostile takeover. UniCredit has pursued Commerzbank for two years and built a stake of nearly 50 percent, alarming Germany, where the bank is a key financing source for small and midsize industrial companies. Berlin and the German lender resisted fiercely. UniCredit plans to use the acquisition to cement its status as a European heavyweight, a goal the European Union shares, and the EU this year announced plans to overhaul merger rules to forge what it calls European champions.
Ranks: customers and firms tied to two large European banks · a cleared cross-border takeover Germany opposed · the approval is in force Source: [uk.finance.yahoo.com](https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/eu-clears-unicredit-takeover-germanys-105424615.html) · [aol.com](https://www.aol.com/articles/unicredit-wins-eu-approval-commerzbank-103548000.html)

**Middle East latest: Tanker struck by unknown projectile in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says: The National**
In the Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO said an unknown projectile struck a tanker.
Ranks: ships using the Strait of Hormuz · one tanker struck · immediate Source: [thenationalnews.com](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2026/11/16/iran-war-live-uss-theodore-roosevelt-middle-east/)

**Jordan bans Telegram app over 'radicalisation' claims: DW World**
Jordan's Public Security Directorate banned Telegram on Monday, saying the app spreads extremism and threatens national interests after a church attack in Karak.

# Omni View Top World News
> **Six Iranian drones targeted a U.S. radar in Bahrain, where sirens warned residents this morning.**

Washington has floated a NATO path for Ukraine if Kyiv left the Donbas, and Australia welcomed a Trump-Xi-Putin summit that Europe wants held without surprises on the war. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Iran targets Bahrain airbase as strikes resume in Gulf: The Guardian**
In Bahrain, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said six drones belonging to its Aerospace Force targeted a U.S. air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base on Sunday. Bahrain's military said it intercepted several Iranian attacks and kept them from their intended targets, while explosions were heard around Manama and authorities posted shelter alerts, their first warnings since September. France 24 reported blasts around 4 a.m. local time and a second series around 6:30 a.m., and said this was the second strike on the island in three days after a lull. The island sits across the Persian Gulf from Iran and hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet; the Guardian says Tehran has hit it repeatedly in a war of flare-ups and long pauses, and France 24 says the energy-rich Gulf has taken the brunt of Iranian strikes. The Guard said the Strait of Hormuz is closed and that any aggression by the United States would meet a harsher, more forceful response. Bahrain's foreign ministry said the kingdom rejects being turned into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible. The Guardian reports talks remain at a stalemate, with Washington keeping a naval blockade and Iran its hold on the strait, while President Donald Trump has threatened major combat and has not returned to it. Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb area, the same coverage says, giving Iran-aligned Houthi fighters greater control of a lane Gulf oil producers had used to move supplies. Hamas said an Israeli strike on Saturday night killed Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade, whom the group said helped plan the 7 October attacks; the BBC, as cited by the Guardian, reported eyewitnesses in Gaza saw four missiles hit a tent in the Al-Waha camp at Al-Mawasi, which shelters hundreds of displaced people. On Friday the Guard said it had targeted a U.S. early-warning radar in Bahrain, the first Gulf strike since early September, and U.S. Central Command said it shot down two Iranian drones with no casualties or damage; the war began on 28 February with U.S.-Israeli strikes that killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and Central Command said last month it had helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels of oil since the summer via Hormuz.
Ranks: Bahrain residents and U.S. forces there · intercepted strike, tighter oil lane · this morning Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/15/middle-east-crisis-live-iran-bahrain-strikes-gulf-donald-trump-us-israel-yemen-houthis)

**Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia?: Al Jazeera**
In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner asked, "What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" Al Jazeera reports the question came at the latest U.S.-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi last week, almost five years into the war. After that round, Witkoff and Kushner met President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Zelenskyy in Dublin before a meeting of European leaders in the Irish capital on Friday. Zelenskyy said NATO is back on the agenda because it sits inside an extremely difficult conversation that would decide the future of European security. He repeated that Kyiv will not give up any of its territories, and he said alliance members had not raised this land-for-membership prospect before. He called the idea dangerous, saying things like it lead to wars or escalations, and that real security in Europe is the European Union and NATO and nothing else. The Kremlin has repeatedly said Ukrainian membership would demand a harsh response, and Putin has demanded that the alliance pull troops back from countries bordering Russia. President Donald Trump had publicly told Ukraine to give up hopes of joining, even as Lithuania and Poland have been among the members most enthusiastic about speeding accession. Ukraine applied in September 2022, months after Russia's full-scale invasion; members remain divided over offering membership during the war, with some seeking an end to the fighting, and raising corruption concerns, as conditions.
Ranks: People in Ukraine and NATO members · a proposal, not an agreed deal · talks already under way Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/15/give-donbas-take-nato-seat-could-new-us-pitch-work-for-ukraine-russia)

**Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit: The Guardian**
In the Philippines, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Sunday in Manila that Australia welcomes this week's planned summit of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. The Guardian reports the three-way meeting is set for Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting, and that European leaders are warning Washington not to make major concessions on Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years after Putin's full-scale invasion, and he has warned the meeting must not become "Yalta 2, 3, 4." Chancellor Friedrich Merz, at a Friday meeting of European Union leaders, said, "please, no surprises," and asked the United States to stay with Europe and Ukraine and work together for a genuine peace. President Emmanuel Macron warned against forcing an unjust peace on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe, calling that the spirit of defeat and a recipe for another war. Albanese said dialogue is a good thing, that the clear message to Putin is the war should end, and that he wants something constructive, including de-escalation in conflicts around the world. He left open joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China, as host, wanted it, and said that if Putin is in a room with him, people will hear his contribution. He said Ukraine's stand is also for the international rule of law, that there are two superpowers, and that the summit would not undercut a push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to carry more weight. On Sunday he signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines while visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila; the Guardian says Australia is helping strengthen Manila's defensive capability against Chinese aggression.
Ranks: Ukraine and the leaders at the table · no bargain yet, Europe asking for no surprises · this week Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/15/anthony-albanese-welcomes-trump-xi-putin-summit-even-as-european-leaders-express-reservations)

**Global diesel prices ease as winter approaches: France 24**
Global diesel prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks, France 24 reports, after staying elevated since the Iran war began and the Strait of Hormuz was blockaded. The network says Gulf exports are recovering and world oil supply is back on track for the first time since February. In the United States, the national average fell below six dollars a gallon on Saturday. In Europe, prices remain roughly seventy-seven percent above pre-war levels even after the drop. The easing is being felt on both sides of the Atlantic as winter approaches. Buyers in Europe are still paying far more than before the war. France 24 ties the change to recovering Gulf exports and supplies getting back on track, not to an end of the fighting. The same war that lifted those prices is the one in which Iran has kept its hold on Hormuz.
Ranks: Drivers in the United States and Europe · prices down, Europe still far above pre-war · this weekend Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/global-diesel-prices-ease-as-winter-approaches)

**Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over fatal church mass shooting: BBC**
In Jordan, a court on Sunday sentenced three men to death by hanging for the 23 October shooting at a funeral at St George's Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hmoud, in Karak governorate. The BBC reports the attack killed nine people and injured thirty-four others; France 24 reported nine killed and twenty-five wounded. Jordan's Armed Forces said the men were convicted of terrorist acts, possessing weapons, promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation, and conspiracy to commit terrorist acts. The three — two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law — have not been publicly identified; they fled, were found in an abandoned house in Karak, and were wounded after they refused to surrender and fired on security forces, who reported no personnel hurt. CCTV showed three men with guns firing on the church, and a second video showed dead and wounded people on the ground; why that church was chosen is still unclear. King Abdullah II wrote after the attack that it would meet the harshest retaliation and that those who thought bullets could divide Jordanians had no chance against unity. The week after the shooting, Jordan said its jets struck what it called terrorist organisations in Syria in retaliation; Syrian health officials told state media five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in a village in southern Daraa province. Jordan said it killed and wounded several terrorists and had coordinated with the Syrian government; Syria said it had not been notified in advance. Christians make up around three percent of the population, Karak has a sizeable Christian community, and executions are by hanging after pauses from 2006 to 2014 and from 2017 until June this year.
Ranks: The Karak community and the three condemned men · death sentences imposed · Sunday's ruling Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rrg9xgqlwpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base: BBC**
In Canada, Private William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday, a month after a fire tore through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, the fifth soldier lost.
Ranks: One soldier's family and his unit · a fifth death from the October fire · Friday Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmrlgn4x2xw8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**The Reward for Black Women's Work in Georgia: Leaders Who Look Like Them: The New York Times**
In the United States, Black women, all Democrats, claimed Georgia offices long held by Republican men.

**Polls open in Cape Verde in race with first female presidential candidate: Al Jazeera**
In Cape Verde, polls opened as Joana Rosa, the first woman candidate, and four opponents face President Jose Maria Neves.

**After Decades of Blood and Mistrust, Doubts Over Who's to Blame for an Israeli Hostage: The New York Times**
In Israel, spies kidnapped and killed Iranians, convinced Tehran was to blame for a fallen airman, the New York Times reports.
Ranks: Families of the missing and of those killed · an old blame claim reopened · no dated next step Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world/europe/ron-arad-missing-israel-iran-asgari-hunt.html)

### Both Sides: Should Ukraine cede the Donbas for a NATO seat?
The United States has put a trade in front of Ukraine: membership in NATO if Kyiv gives up the whole Donbas. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised it with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at talks in Abu Dhabi, he told reporters on Saturday, in the question, "What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" They then met President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday and briefed Zelenskyy in Dublin before European leaders gathered there on Friday.

Zelenskyy's case against giving up land is that Kyiv will not hand over any territory. His best reason, as he stated it, is security: real security in Europe is the European Union and NATO, and a bargain that swaps land for membership can itself cause war. He said alliance members had not put that question before, and he called the idea dangerous because such proposals lead to wars or escalations. Ukraine applied to join in September 2022 to fortify its border after Russia's full-scale invasion.

The case for even asking, as Washington framed it, is that NATO membership is the guarantee Kyiv has sought for almost five years, and that Putin has made all of the Donbas a condition for ending the war. The Kremlin's reason for rejecting the NATO half is that Ukrainian membership would demand a harsh response, and that the alliance should pull forces back from states on Russia's border. President Donald Trump had, until this pitch, told Ukraine in public to abandon joining. Lithuania and Poland have been among the members most eager to speed accession, while other members remain divided and some want the war ended first.

No decision date is set. The same negotiators have already sat with Putin and with European leaders, and a separate Trump-Xi-Putin meeting is planned this week in Shenzhen, where Zelenskyy has warned against any redistribution of influence that leaves Ukraine behind.

### Progress Watch
SpaceX recaptured its massive reusable rocket ship, Starship, for the first time, France 24 reports, a day after a catch attempt on a booster failed. Smaller earlier models have landed again, but they need heavy legs and are not fully reusable. Sunday's catch is a completed flight result, not a plan. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/spacex-makes-rocketry-history-by-recapturing-massive-reusable-rocketship)

# Omni View Top World News
> **More than eight thousand two hundred U.S. flights were canceled Friday, stranding passengers nationwide.**

The Federal Aviation Administration’s rare nationwide ground stop, the longest of its kind in the country since September 11, 2001, has been lifted, while airlines and airports were still working through the delays. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**What to Know About Friday’s Nationwide Ground Stop: The New York Times**

The United States stopped departures across the country on Friday afternoon. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop after outdated air-traffic communications equipment became overloaded with data and began to fail, The New York Times reported. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters at the White House on Friday night that radar and other air-traffic communications started to falter at 3:36 p.m., when old routers became overloaded with data. He said the failures were not universal. He said they were pervasive enough that officials issued an unusual nationwide moratorium on takeoffs.

France 24 reported the scale of what that moratorium did to the day’s flying. More than 8,200 flights were canceled. That was over 31 percent of the flights scheduled in the United States. The ground stop lasted nearly five hours. France 24 said it was the longest nationwide ground stop in the country since September 11, 2001. Officials blamed outdated air-traffic communications equipment. France 24 said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. The airspace has since reopened, and flights have resumed.

The Times described what the stop left behind once the clock on those nearly five hours had run. The outage stranded thousands of passengers. It caused widespread delays. Airlines and airports were still struggling to recover from those delays. The afternoon, the Times wrote, highlighted persistent vulnerabilities in the aging U.S. air-traffic infrastructure. It also opened a funding fight. Administration officials demanded that lawmakers approve tens of billions of dollars more to accelerate systemwide upgrades. That demand is a request put to Congress. It is not an appropriation. It is not a completed upgrade. No vote on the demand is reported in today’s articles.

Two officials who appeared together at the White House drew different lines around the same failure. Duffy insisted that the failure was caused by the antiquated, legacy communications equipment, not by recent upgrades to the system. Markwayne Mullin, whom the Times identified as the homeland security secretary, stood with him. Mullin said investigators had seen zero evidence that a cyberattack triggered the technology failures. He suggested that new equipment and new technology Duffy’s department had added to the old infrastructure was what had overwhelmed it. France 24’s account, that officials blamed outdated communications equipment, sits beside that split. Neither official described a finding that every communications site had failed. Both described a failure wide enough to stop departures everywhere. Duffy’s 3:36 p.m. mark is the time he gave for the start of the faltering, not the time the stop was lifted. France 24’s nearly five hours is the length of the ground stop. Together they place the failure in a Friday afternoon and evening, when a national hold on takeoffs hits the day’s remaining departures at once.

For a passenger booked on one of the canceled flights, the change was immediate: a departure that did not leave, then a restart into a system already out of position. For an airline, more than 8,200 cancellations in one country, on one day, is not a local weather bank. It is a broken schedule at national scale, with aircraft, crews and connecting passengers left in the wrong places when the hold lifted. The Times’ account that carriers and airports were still struggling to recover is the part that outlasts the nearly five hours of the stop itself. A ground stop ends when takeoffs are allowed again. The delays it creates keep moving through later banks of flights. France 24’s report that flights have resumed and the Times’ report that recovery was unfinished can both be true at once: the moratorium is over, and the timetable is not yet whole.

The share France 24 gave — over 31 percent of flights scheduled in the United States — is a share of the day’s U.S. schedule, not a count of people. The Times’ figure for people is thousands of passengers stranded. The articles do not convert either number into a single total of travelers turned away. What they do fix is the reach of the order: a moratorium on takeoffs that was nationwide, unusual, and long enough for France 24 to set it against the ground stop of September 11, 2001, as the longest of its kind in the country since that day.

What the episode changes, beyond those hours, is the argument over the equipment the country flies on. The Times tied the stop to vulnerabilities that officials already describe as persistent, and to a demand for tens of billions of dollars more so that systemwide upgrades can move faster. Duffy’s account points that money at replacing legacy routers and communications gear he says failed on their own. Mullin’s account points it at a different risk: new technology added onto old infrastructure, overloading what was already there. The listener does not have, in either official’s remarks as published, a joint finding that settles which account is the operating one. What both put on the record is the absence, in their telling, of evidence of a cyberattack, and the presence of a failure serious enough to stop takeoffs nationwide.

The next step the articles name is the one already taken and the one still asked for. The stop has been lifted, and flights have resumed. Until Congress acts or declines to act, the system that failed on Friday afternoon is the system airlines are using to rebuild Friday’s broken day. That is the consequence that does not wait on the argument: people who were meant to fly did not, crews and aircraft are still being put back in order, and the officials responsible for the network disagree, in public, about whether the failure was the old equipment or the new gear laid on top of it.

Ranks: travelers on more than 8,200 canceled U.S. flights, and the airports and airlines rebuilding those schedules · a national halt on takeoffs lasting nearly five hours, with recovery still unfinished · already under way since Friday afternoon Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-stop-flights-what-to-know.html)
Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/us-nationwide-flight-ground-stop-our-routers-got-overloaded-with-data)

### Both Sides: What overloaded U.S. air-traffic communications
What is being decided is not whether Friday’s stop happened. It happened. What is in dispute is the mechanism of that nationwide ground stop, and therefore what tens of billions of dollars in faster upgrades would be buying. The Federal Aviation Administration ordered the stop after communications equipment overloaded with data and began to fail. No vote on that demand, and no date for one, is reported in today’s articles. The operational next step is already on the record: the airspace has reopened and flights have resumed, while airlines and airports were still struggling to recover.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters at the White House on Friday night that radar and other communications started to falter at 3:36 p.m. when old routers became overloaded with data. His case is that the failure belongs to antiquated, legacy communications equipment. He insisted it was not caused by recent upgrades. On that account, the reason to spend is to replace gear that has already shown it can force a nationwide moratorium on takeoffs. France 24 called that stop the longest in the country since September 11, 2001, and reported more than 8,200 flights canceled, over 31 percent of those scheduled in the United States. Duffy also said the failures were not universal, only pervasive enough to justify stopping takeoffs everywhere. His strongest reason, stated in his own terms, is that the old routers overloaded, and that recent upgrades were not the cause.

Markwayne Mullin, identified by the Times as the homeland security secretary, made the other case while standing with Duffy. On that account, the risk is not only age. It is the way new systems are laid onto old ones. A large new appropriation, spent the same way, could repeat the overload rather than end it. His strongest reason is the one he offered at the White House: the added technology, not a hostile intrusion, is what he suggested had overwhelmed the old infrastructure.

France 24 reported that officials blamed outdated air-traffic communications equipment and said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. That reporting aligns with Duffy on age and with both men on the cyber question. It does not choose between Duffy’s rejection of recent upgrades and Mullin’s suggestion that added technology was the overload. The listener is left with two official accounts of one Friday afternoon, a canceled share of the U.S. schedule above 31 percent, a stop of nearly five hours, and a funding demand whose size the Times put at tens of billions of dollars more, still unvoted in these reports. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-stop-flights-what-to-know.html)
Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/us-nationwide-flight-ground-stop-our-routers-got-overloaded-with-data)

### Progress Watch
Microsoft said on Saturday morning that it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions hit by one of the worst information-technology failures in years. On its Microsoft 365 status page, the company said it had completed its efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. The Guardian reported that Microsoft described the service as fully restored after a massive outage that caused widespread disruption to governments, businesses and public services around the world.

The company said the outage had affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hours-long episode had affected some of their operations. In the United Kingdom, hospital staff resorted to paper records and courtrooms scrambled to locate fax machines. Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and the artificial-intelligence assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories, and that it received reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour after problems first emerged.

Microsoft said on its website that more than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps. The company said in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services. The Guardian said the total number of people affected was not the figure those subscription counts settle; the counts are Microsoft’s own measures of the installed base the outage could reach. Problems started appearing at about midday on Thursday in the United States and 6 p.m. in the United Kingdom. The Washington-based company apologised on Friday. It said the outage was not related to cyber or to artificial-intelligence agents. It said the incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change.

The restoration is the measured change: a failure Microsoft itself ranked among the worst information-technology failures in years, declared over for the remaining customers and regions on Saturday morning. What the same reporting leaves in place is the dependence the outage made visible. The Guardian said the disruptions were the latest example of cascading problems when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider, and that the outage fuelled concerns in the United Kingdom about an over-reliance on a small number of technology companies. Tim Clement-Jones, a former chair of the House of Lords artificial-intelligence select committee, called the widespread outages of vital government services an “I told you so moment” highlighting Britain’s dependence on U.S. technology. Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s school of computing science, said the problem emphasised the dependence built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and might lead people to question whether more resilience is needed in the information-technology ecosystem. Those are arguments about what should follow a restoration Microsoft says is already complete. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/14/microsoft-says-services-fully-restored-after-global-outage)
