# Omni View Top World News
> **Seventy thousand tents flooded in Gaza, leaving displaced families without shelter tonight.**

**What You Need to Know:** Heavy rain has flooded seventy thousand tents across the Gaza Strip, and displaced families are without adequate shelter. Missiles aimed at Riyadh damaged a Saudi Aramco building, climate talks open in Antalya, and a gunman killed six people in Kraków. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Storm floods tens of thousands of tents across war-ravaged Gaza: The Arab Weekly**
In the Gaza Strip, heavy rain and strong winds since late Friday flooded shelters used by displaced Palestinians, Al Jazeera reported, and France 24 said the water reached camps in Deir al-Balah as well as elsewhere in the territory. The Government Media Office said the storm flooded 70,000 tents and brought down dozens of walls, and it estimated the damage at $3 million. Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili, reporting from Gaza City, said the makeshift tents do not keep out harsh weather, that wind and rain tore through shelters families had spent days trying to reinforce, and that he saw soaked mattresses, pillows and clothes. He said nearly 400,000 displaced Palestinians are sheltering in locations considered highly vulnerable to more flooding. From Deir el-Balah, Al Jazeera’s Ashraf Abu Amra said families whose shelters flooded had not received food aid since early Saturday. France 24 reported that residents said overflowing sewage had mixed with the floodwater, and that families were building earthen barriers and draining water by hand after essential belongings were soaked. The Gaza Civil Defence said it received at least 1,500 emergency calls, that more than 2,000 buildings are at risk of collapse, and that at least 300,000 tents are needed for adequate shelter. Jonathan Veitch, UNICEF’s special representative in Palestine, said most people are living in terrible conditions and called for more funding, while relief groups have struggled for years to bring supplies in. Al Jazeera reported that Israel continues to impose severe restrictions on aid, shelter supplies and reconstruction materials. Al Jazeera also reported that more than 74,640 people have been killed since 7 October 2023, and that Israel has killed at least 1,610 Palestinians since a ceasefire took effect in October 2025.
Ranks: Displaced people in Gaza, in the hundreds of thousands · shelters flooded and aid still tightly limited · already, with more rain a risk Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8/floods-in-gaza-leave-tens-of-thousands-without-shelter?traffic_source=rss)
Source: [thearabweekly.com](https://thearabweekly.com/storm-floods-tens-thousands-tents-across-war-ravaged-gaza)

**Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged in ‘attempted’ attack: Al Jazeera**
In Saudi Arabia, an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was damaged by falling shrapnel, with no injuries or fatalities, the energy ministry said through state media on Sunday, after an attempted attack. Several news agencies reported damage to a tower in the King Abdullah Financial District. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences destroyed several ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis. Spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said two missiles were launched toward Riyadh, another targeted the Eastern Province, and that defences also destroyed two missiles in the south and a drone. France 24 reported that the Aramco Tower was damaged by falling debris after two ballistic missiles headed for the capital’s financial district were intercepted. A day earlier, Yemen’s Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi-led air strikes killed at least 33 people, including eight women and 13 children, in the village of al-Shariyah in the Bani Hushaish district near Sanaa, and wounded at least 39, hitting homes, roads, paramedics and civil defence teams. France 24’s live account stated the same death toll from Saturday’s strikes on Bani Hushaysh and said most of those killed were women and children. Hospital director Abdul-Aziz al-Dailami said many victims remained under rubble, including first responders. The coalition had no immediate comment, and Al Jazeera said it could not independently verify that toll. On Friday an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people: the Houthis blamed Saudi air strikes, while Yemeni government forces accused the Houthis of firing a ballistic missile. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the coalition carried out 105 air strikes and missile attacks in 24 hours on Sanaa and seven other governorates, taking the total since the escalation began to 4,369. The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and almost 300,000 displaced since a 2022 ceasefire collapsed in July, after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports. Al Jazeera reported that the Houthis have hit Saudi airports, the Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and other Aramco sites since that collapse, and that at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in a Houthi strike on Riyadh airport on 10 October.
Ranks: People in Yemen and in Riyadh, hundreds of thousands already displaced · a damaged oil building and disputed civilian deaths · immediate Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8/saudi-arabia-intercepts-houthi-missiles-targeting-riyadh-eastern-province)
Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20261108-middle-east-live-riyadh-financial-district-targeted-deadly-strikes-yemen-israel-eisenkot-netanyahu-coalition-government-elections)

**US launches task force to disrupt land transit routes into Iran: France 24**
The United States military has announced a 20-member task force to find ways to disrupt land routes into Iran that it says are used for shipments of weapons and illicit materials, France 24 reported. US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a statement posted on Saturday that the work will further constrain Iran’s ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories and replenish its military. The team of civilian and military personnel, based in Florida, would coordinate with US government agencies on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea. The restrictions would expand a US naval blockade of Iranian ports during the two countries’ eight-month war. Tehran has also restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, choking global energy supplies. Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi, quoted by the semi-official Fars news agency, said the Iron Gate plan is merely wordplay and that the Americans cannot achieve economic collapse in Iran this way, because Tehran has made preparations and communicates closely with neighbours. Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said on Sunday at a ceremony that the mission regarding Iran is still not complete. He charged that Iran is trying to renew efforts to obtain nuclear weapons, which the Islamic republic has long denied, alongside other efforts he said place Israel in real danger.
Ranks: Oil buyers and people living with the Iran war, a global set · a wider blockade, if it works · starting now, over months Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20261108-middle-east-live-riyadh-financial-district-targeted-deadly-strikes-yemen-israel-eisenkot-netanyahu-coalition-government-elections)

**Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks: The Guardian**
In Turkey, the COP31 climate summit opens on Monday in Antalya, with Australia in charge of the negotiations after a bitter hosting row with Turkey, the Guardian reported, and Anadolu Agency said the talks kick off that day. Hosting the summit was a pledge from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in 2021, while he was still in opposition. Arcane rules made Australia wait its turn to bid, and the compromise put the talks in the Turkish city while leaving Australia to run them. Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment and is unlikely to stay long, and Australian media has been quieter than in previous host countries. Climate and energy minister Chris Bowen will be in daily charge of the negotiations, while parts of Australia’s energy supply also sit in his portfolio, so he has had to boost fossil fuels while insisting on a clean-energy transition. The Guardian said Australia remains a major fossil-fuel exporter and has also invested heavily in renewables, to the point that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan showed little interest in climate before bidding to host. In the last five years the summit has also been held in Egypt, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan, which the Guardian said has given the Arab group an outsize role and a strong interest in fossil-fuel representation, including lobbyists. Environment minister Murat Kurum controls the action agenda of voluntary initiatives, which Erdoğan has used to advance his wife Emine Erdoğan’s push to cut waste and promote a circular economy. She has called for an end to throwaway culture and for recycling instead of landfill, though Turkey still has sites that leak vast quantities of methane. Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency, is understood to be among the advisers behind this year’s emphasis on electrification for heating, transport and industry, which could halve the energy needed after renewable generation is expanded. Brazil’s re-elected president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will come for his first trip abroad after winning a fourth term and will bring two non-binding roadmaps, one on a transition away from fossil fuels and one on halting and reversing deforestation, with no deadlines or firm requirements on governments. President Xi Jinping will not attend. China is the world’s second-biggest economy and the biggest emitter, making up nearly a third of annual global carbon output, mainly from fossil fuels used in 25 years of rapid growth, while its renewable investment is also reshaping the energy business. The officials he sends will know that Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are important allies.
Ranks: Governments at the talks, and people exposed to a hotter climate · the agenda for this round of talks, not a new treaty yet · from Monday Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/08/cop31-key-players-climate-talks)
Source: [aa.com.tr](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/turkiye/cop31-climate-summit-to-kick-off-in-turkiyes-antalya-on-monday/4115777)

**Briton among six dead after gunman opens fire in Kraków market square: The Guardian**
In Poland, a gunman opened fire with an automatic weapon in Kraków’s main market square at about 3 p.m. on Saturday, the Guardian reported. Authorities said six people were killed and 16 wounded in what was a busy square. A Briton was among the six dead. Three more people were found dead at the home of the suspect. The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, was apprehended by police. Poland’s defence minister called the shooting an act of terror on the people of the city. The minister said the suspect held ultra-nationalistic views. BBC Verify authenticated video showing the moment the gunshots rang out in the square.
Ranks: People in Kraków’s main square, and the dead and wounded · six killed, sixteen wounded, three more dead at a home · already Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shooting-market-square-deaths-gunman)
Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cq74p2zpwyjmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Eisenkot, Netanyahu Rival and Opposition Leader, Tapped to Try to Form Government: The New York Times**
In Israel, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is seeking to form a government after an inconclusive election, the New York Times reported.
Ranks: Israelis choosing a government · who gets the first chance to bargain · this week Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/world/middleeast/israel-eisenkot-government.html)
Source: [nbcnews.com](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/middle-east/israel-mired-uncertainty-acrimony-contentious-vote-rcna607382)

**In Argentina, Pope Leo to Meet Church at Odds With President Milei: The New York Times**
In Argentina, Pope Leo’s trip comes amid tensions between libertarian leader Javier Milei and the Catholic Church, the New York Times reported.
Ranks: Argentina’s church and government · a public clash of priorities · from Monday Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/world/americas/pope-leo-argentina-milei.html)

**Final ballot count to determine fate of close local races starts this week: Dayton Daily News**
In Ohio, officials will count 4,418 provisional ballots that could decide a race Republican Tom Young trails by 134 votes.
Ranks: Voters in one Ohio county · a House seat and a school levy still open · this week, through 24 November Source: [daytondailynews.com](https://www.daytondailynews.com/local/final-ballot-count-to-determine-fate-of-close-local-races-starts-this-week/article_49898678-40ad-557f-8333-2f477876c83a.html)

**Is NC turning blue? Not so fast. What this year’s election results results mean for 2028: WRAL**
In North Carolina, Roy Cooper beat Michael Whatley for the Senate by about 20 points, the first Democratic win there since 2008.
Ranks: North Carolina’s Senate voters · one seat changes hands · already decided Source: [wral.com](https://www.wral.com/news/nccapitol/north-carolina-turning-blue-election-results-forecast-2028-november-8/)

**Matt Witt: This Veterans Day, let’s focus on preventing war: Pioneer Press**
In the United States, Donald Trump said on Truth Social that Veterans Day should become Victory Day for World War I.
Ranks: Americans marking 11 November · a proposed new name, not yet a statute in this report · before the holiday Source: [twincities.com](https://www.twincities.com/2026/11/08/matt-witt-this-veterans-day-lets-focus-on-preventing-war/)

### Both Sides: Who is responsible for the latest civilian deaths in Yemen?
The question is whether the Saudi-led coalition should keep striking inside Yemen after a weekend in which each side blamed the other for civilian deaths. The coalition’s case, put by spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki, is that Houthi missiles were already in the air: he said two were launched toward Riyadh, another targeted the Eastern Province, and that defences destroyed those plus two missiles in the south and a drone. The energy ministry said falling shrapnel from that attempted attack damaged an Aramco administrative building and killed no one. Stopping those launches, on this account, is what the air campaign is for. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree has described a widening exchange, claiming 105 coalition strikes and missile attacks in 24 hours and 4,369 since the escalation began. The other case, from the Houthi-run health ministry and spokesman Anees al-Asbahi, is that coalition aircraft killed 33 people on Saturday in al-Shariyah near Sanaa, including eight women and 13 children, and wounded at least 39, hitting homes, roads, paramedics and civil defence teams. France 24 stated that toll as the result of Saturday’s strikes and said most of those killed were women and children. On the Taiz market attack that killed 30 on Friday, the Houthis blamed Saudi strikes, while Yemeni government forces said the Houthis fired a ballistic missile. No article sets a date for a joint investigation or a new truce. The United Nations’ count since the July collapse of the 2022 ceasefire — more than 1,600 killed and almost 300,000 displaced — is the scale both claims now sit against.

### Progress Watch
**Solar power in Australia has expanded so far that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity, the Guardian reported, even while the country remains a major fossil-fuel exporter.** Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/08/cop31-key-players-climate-talks)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Two chambers of Congress flipped to Democrats, checking Trump on tariffs and the Iran war.**

The new majority can legislate and investigate, but it lacks the votes to override a veto, while strikes continue and Tehran says the Strait of Hormuz stays shut. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Five ways the midterm election results could reshape Donald Trump's America: The Globe and Mail**

The United States has a Congress no longer run by President Donald Trump's party, and the argument over what that majority can do is already about prices, tariffs and a war. The Globe and Mail reported that this week's midterm vote swept Republicans from power and that Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. VPM News said Democrats won strong majorities in both chambers. The Globe and Mail called the result a political upheaval unlike any seen in generations, and framed the morning after as revival for Democrats and a deepening political dusk for Mr. Trump.

For the past two years, the Globe and Mail wrote, Congress under Republican control largely stood as a passive bystander to Mr. Trump. Democratic control, in that account, gives the party strength to pass legislation, reject judges, investigate wrongdoing and counter attempts by the president to rule by executive fiat. The same report states the limit in the same breath: Democrats hold insufficient numbers to overcome his veto. The paper asks, without answering, whether the country gets a hard-fought stalemate between branches seeking mutual obstruction, or room to address living costs, corruption and federal debt grown to astronomical proportions, while both parties prepare for the end of his presidency. It said five themes are likely to dominate the new day. The first is cost.

Senate Leader Chuck Schumer promised this week that the first priority for victorious Democrats is to "reduce people's costs and work the legislative process so it does." He did not say how. Candidates had spent months decrying tariffs, and some returned to that theme on election night as they began looking toward a legislative agenda. Sherrod Brown in Ohio said, "We will fight to end these tariffs." Josh Turek in Iowa said Mr. Trump's tariffs "are decimating markets, killing farmers and hurting our rural communities." Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932, said every Kansan has been "hurt by the tariffs." Those are campaign and leadership statements, not statutes.

The tariff map, as the Globe and Mail sets it out, is wide. Mr. Trump has levied tariffs on about 60 countries under the auspices of seeking to eliminate "forced labour" from countries such as Switzerland and Canada, in addition to a raft of measures on metals and vehicles and, more recently, 50 per cent taxes on tens of billions of dollars in imports from Canada, the northern neighbour. Democrats, the paper wrote, have little choice but to try to reverse some of those measures, because the campaign was built on the cost of them.

Democratic campaign strategist Chuck Rocha worked on campaigns that won 21 Congressional seats in the midterm vote. He made 251 ads, virtually all of them on cost, corruption and the overreach of immigration enforcement. In many, he said, "we put the tariffs and the war in the same ads, as the two reasons driving up cost." For that reason alone, he said, "I do think Congress will do something around tariffs." He also named the constraint in the next breath: "The problem with the tariff argument is that the President has so much control over tariffs." On whether lawmakers can force a change, he said, "I don't know the legality policy-wise." Democrats have said they are determined to try.

Jamie Raskin, a Maryland congressman, told CBC's Canadian audience that Congress would tackle tariffs "within the first 100 days" of the party's return to legislative power. Ron Wyden, a Democratic senator from Oregon, told The Wall Street Journal: "There is overwhelming support for repealing the tariffs on products from Canada." One option the Globe and Mail describes is to strike down the legal authority used by the White House to tax imports. An obvious candidate, the paper says, would be Section 338, the provision under the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act that Mr. Trump used for the first time in U.S. history to impose 50-per-cent tariffs on goods from Canada this year. Congress could also codify the Supreme Court decision that struck down his earlier use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose tariffs. Neither step has been taken. No repeal vote is on a calendar in these reports. Raskin's clock is a promise of the first 100 days, not a scheduled sitting.

The New York Times reported a separate caution for Canada: while U.S. voters largely oppose the trade war with Canada, many Democrats and their supporters have protectionist leanings, and America's rebuke of Mr. Trump will not swiftly restore Canada-U.S. harmony. That is the paper's reading of the new majority, not a finding that a tariff bill has failed. France 24 reported that, in this era of divided government, Democratic lawmakers say their priorities will be tackling the rising cost of living, investigating alleged corruption, and tightening oversight of ICE agents. Antonia Kerrigan reported that account. Alleged corruption is the word the lawmakers' stated priority uses; the reports here do not set out a charge, a defendant or a finding.

The White House answered the vote with a staff change, not a tariff retreat. The Guardian reported that on Friday afternoon Mr. Trump abruptly announced on his Truth Social platform that Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, and that he confirmed Wiles had been ousted. The Guardian describes Miller as his most trusted adviser and as the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, the record the appointment puts at the centre of the West Wing. It reported that Democrats and Republicans blasted the promotion. Trump explaining the change beyond the announcement that Wiles was out and Miller was in.

Virginia, in VPM News's tally, did not move as one bloc even as the national count did. The Associated Press called the 1st Congressional District for Democrat Shannon Taylor over longtime Republican Representative Rob Wittman; VPM said that call came Thursday, with Keyris Manzanares reporting it. Republican Representative John McGuire held the 5th against Tom Perriello. Billy Shields reported that McGuire withstood what VPM called the national blue wave and retained the seat. Eugene Vindman won reelection in Virginia's 7th District. Voters signed off on all three constitutional amendments. On Tuesday night Jahd Khalil, recording from his car in Henrico County, reported voters approving those three state amendments. VPM aired Governor Abigail Spanberger, at a virtual press conference, talking about a statewide shift toward Democrats, and reported Jackie McDonnough's win in a Richmond School Board race as unexpected. Gregory Six won a special election to remain Hanover County sheriff.

Certification is still a process, not a finished national headline. VPM explained that before winners are declared, local election officers review and verify the totals for each voting machine. Those totals are collected and given to the general registrar and the local electoral board. Local electoral boards certify results and declare winners for local offices and issues. The State Board of Elections verifies statewide races, constitutional amendments, General Assembly elections and federal races such as Congress. Electoral Board Chair Bill Pantele said of the Richmond canvass, "It's done when it's done, and when it's done right." He said the board would work through the weekend if that is what it takes, because November elections with higher turnouts mean more work, including provisional and absentee ballots as well as regular votes. Much of the national attention on Tuesday night, VPM noted, sat on Congress; by Wednesday, Richmond's job was canvassing and verifying what was cast locally.

The war that Rocha put beside tariffs in those ads is still being fought, and Saturday's reporting is about strikes and a waterway, not about a ceasefire. ASHARQ AL-AWSAT, citing army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia through the state news agency IRNA, reported that Iran's military is "stronger" and more motivated than when the United States and Israel started the war in February. Akraminia said, according to IRNA: "Today, the Islamic Republic's armed forces... having gained experience from direct confrontation with the United States and the Israeli regime, are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war." He added that they "now possess greater motivation, commitment, and self-confidence." The war began when the United States and Israel carried out a massive wave of strikes in late February and has been deadlocked for months.

Tehran has sought to limit traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption. According to AFP, as carried by ASHARQ AL-AWSAT, Akraminia said Iranian armed forces retained control over the strategic waterway and that it would remain closed until the United States accepted Tehran's demands. That is the spokesman's claim about control and about a condition for reopening, not a published shipping tally. Under the order of the Supreme Leader, he added, "the response of the armed forces will be immediate, effective, and without geographical limitations."

President Trump this week confirmed new strikes on Iran, after American media reported attacks on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. On Saturday the local Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm, adding that there was no official information so far on the damage. Iranian state television reported two explosions on the island. The Iranian army said early Saturday that its air defenses had "struck and destroyed" a U.S. drone that was flying over the island, according to state media. It did not say whether the island was attacked. Those are three accounts of the same morning: a presidential confirmation of new strikes, a local agency's report of two missiles with no official damage figure, and an army claim, via state media, that a drone was destroyed.

Anadolu Ajansı reported that Australia's premier urged the United States to de-escalate the Iran war after the Republican midterm losses. EA WorldView reported that its correspondent, speaking with Pakistan TV's Sana Maqbool, set out the vote's significance for Vice President J.D. Vance, described as an opponent of the war from its launch, who proposed reopening talks to Iran. The correspondent considered the possibility that the United States and Iran may converge on a settlement allowing Tehran to continue enriching uranium, albeit at lower levels, in exchange for significant relief from U.S. sanctions. The correspondent said that shape would resemble the 2015 nuclear agreement between Iran and the 5+1 powers, including the United States, the agreement the correspondent said Mr. Trump ripped up in 2018. That is an analyst's reading of a possible bargain, not a text tabled by either capital. The same piece's photograph caption places Mr. Vance before a quadrilateral meeting of the United States, Iran, Pakistan and Qatar at the Burgenstock resort above Lake Lucerne on June 21, 2026. No new round is dated in Saturday's reports.

What changes, and for whom, is therefore split by institution and by clock. Importers paying the Canadian tariff line, and the farmers and rural buyers named by Brown, Turek and Hamilton, are the people Democratic leaders say a cost bill would reach, if one is written inside Raskin's 100 days and if it survives a veto the Globe and Mail says this majority cannot override. Oil buyers are the people named by the scale of the strait: about one-fifth of global oil consumption normally moves there, and Tehran's army spokesman says the waterway stays under Iranian control until Washington accepts Iranian demands, while Washington has confirmed further strikes. Staff in the West Wing change now: Miller in, Wiles out, as of Friday's announcement. Virginia's local boards are still in the canvass, with Pantele's weekend as the near date, and the State Board still to verify the federal races. None of the outlets above reports a signed repeal, a ceasefire, or a date for talks.

Ranks: Voters, importers and oil buyers in the United States, Canada and beyond · a majority that can legislate and investigate but cannot override a veto, beside a war still claimed to be closing a strait that carries about one-fifth of global oil · immediate for staffing and strikes, and inside a stated first hundred days for any tariff bill Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-five-ways-midterm-election-results-reshape-united-states-donald-trump/) · [vpm.org](https://www.vpm.org/news/2026-11-07/vpm-news-top-stories-nov-7-2026/) · [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-democrats-react) · [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/usa-democrats-vow-to-investigate-donald-trump) · [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/world/canada/carney-trump-canada-us-relations-midterm-elections.html) · [english.aawsat.com](https://english.aawsat.com/world/5338484-army-spokesman-iranian-forces-stronger-beginning-war) · [eaworldview.com](https://eaworldview.com/2026/11/iran-war-after-us-elections/) · [aa.com.tr](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/asia-pacific/australian-premier-urges-us-to-de-escalate-iran-war-after-republican-midterm-losses/4115042)

### Both Sides: Repealing tariffs on Canadian goods
The decision in front of the new Congress is whether to repeal President Donald Trump's tariffs on goods from Canada, and whether it has a legal path that survives the presidency.

The case for repeal, as Democrats stated it, starts with household and farm costs rather than with a drafted statute. Chuck Schumer said the first priority is to reduce people's costs through the legislative process. Sherrod Brown said Democrats will fight to end the tariffs. Josh Turek said the tariffs are decimating markets, killing farmers and hurting rural communities. Adam Hamilton said every Kansan has been hurt by them. Ron Wyden told The Wall Street Journal there is overwhelming support for repealing the tariffs on products from Canada. Chuck Rocha said tariffs and the war were paired in ads as the two reasons driving up cost, which is why he thinks Congress will act. Their shared reason is price: the tariffs, in this telling, are a cause of the costs the new majority was elected to cut.

The case for leaving the tariffs where they are rests on the purpose under which they were imposed and on who holds the pen. The Globe and Mail reported that Mr. Trump levied tariffs on about 60 countries under the auspices of seeking to eliminate forced labour from countries including Switzerland and Canada, and that this year's 50 per cent taxes on tens of billions of dollars in Canadian imports used Section 338 of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act for the first time in U.S. history. Rocha, who expects Congress to try, said the president has so much control over tariffs that he does not know the legality of a congressional change. The New York Times reported that many Democrats and their supporters have protectionist leanings even while U.S. voters largely oppose the trade war with Canada, and that the election will not swiftly restore harmony. The Globe and Mail also reported that Democrats lack the numbers to overcome a veto, so a repeal that passes one or both chambers can still stop at the White House. That limit is arithmetic in the paper's account, not a prediction of how Mr. Trump would use it.

No vote is dated. Raskin's clock is the first 100 days. Wyden described support, not a bill number. Schumer did not say how costs would come down. A Supreme Court decision has already struck down an earlier tariff use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, and the Globe and Mail says Congress could codify that ruling, or could try to strike Section 338. Both remain options on paper. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-five-ways-midterm-election-results-reshape-united-states-donald-trump/) · [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/world/canada/carney-trump-canada-us-relations-midterm-elections.html)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Forty-seven billion dollars and twenty-three American deaths mark eight months of the Iran war.**

**What You Need to Know:** Forty-seven billion dollars and twenty-three American deaths mark eight months of the Iran war, with the Pentagon also counting more than 850 U.S. troops injured as of October 30. Elsewhere, a Tanzanian court jailed the main opposition leader for four years after acquitting him of treason, and Britain’s prime minister said employers will have to show pay on job ads. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Iran War passes 8-month mark: WLWT**
The war with Iran has passed its eighth month, and Pentagon figures now put a casualty count and a dollar cost on it for Congress and for U.S. forces. Twenty-three U.S. service members have died and more than 850 have been injured, according to Pentagon data as of October 30, WLWT reports. The latest Pentagon estimate to Congress puts the war’s cost at 47.1 billion dollars. WLWT says that bill is reaching U.S. consumers in everything from gas to mortgages. President Donald Trump has said the war will end when he can ensure that Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. At a campaign rally in Georgia two weekends ago, Trump said the country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what is happening in the Middle East, and that pump prices are going to come down, West Virginia Watch reports. He told that crowd he did not care if the headline was that he was talking about the money while people suffered at the pump, and said, “We’re making a freaking fortune.” That column reports that on Friday ExxonMobil’s profits doubled from the same period last year and Chevron’s nearly tripled. It says a major oil shipping lane has been closed, gas prices have risen, high diesel costs have lifted the price of goods through transport, and October inflation numbers were higher than usual. The columnist asks who is taking that fortune while U.S. soldiers have died and civilians in Iran and other Middle Eastern countries have died, and says national leaders are boasting of corporate profits while cutting food assistance and healthcare.
Ranks: U.S. forces, consumers, and people living with the war · billions in cost, deaths, and higher prices · already, with no end date set Source: [wlwt.com](https://www.wlwt.com/article/iran-war-timeline/74294888) Source: [westvirginiawatch.com](https://westvirginiawatch.com/2026/11/06/west-virginians-footing-the-bill-for-war-and-big-oil/)

**Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason: BBC**
In Tanzania, the High Court in Dar es Salaam found opposition leader Tundu Lissu guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced him to four years in jail, the BBC reports. A panel of three judges acquitted the 58-year-old of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge. Treason is among the country’s most serious offences and can carry the death penalty. Lissu, who leads Chadema and has been detained since April last year, denied the charges and called the prosecution politically motivated. He was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign for changes to the electoral system. The court said his slogan “No Reforms, No Election” was enough for an incitement conviction, ruling that by uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them he incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections. Lissu told the judges they had manufactured an offence that did not exist, on political directives, and said he had been charged only with treason, not incitement. He said he would apply for bail, which he said is available for incitement but not for treason, and he has leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. A lawyer who represented himself, he argued that his remarks, also circulated online, were a lawful campaign, and that prosecutors had taken them out of context. Chadema’s demands included independently appointed electoral commissioners, police allowing parties to campaign free of intimidation, an end to government-appointed district chiefs acting as returning officers, party agents observing the count without harassment, and a right to challenge presidential results in court. President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98 percent of the vote, a result the opposition called a mockery of democracy after her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded; her government has repeatedly denied targeting opponents. In remand at Ukonga Prison he went on hunger strike twice for brief periods, saying he was denied access to lawyers or relatives and that guards listened to consultations; the prison authorities have denied those allegations.
Ranks: Tanzania’s opposition and voters in a disputed election · a four-year sentence, treason dropped · sentence now, appeal still open Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp8g4pm0y4lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Employers to be forced to put salaries on job ads, Andy Burnham announces: The Guardian**
In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his government will make it a legal requirement for employers to state what they pay when they list jobs, the Guardian reports. He said a young person starting out, or a parent supporting a family, should know the pay before spending time on an application. Officials say publishing pay will also help people already in work see whether they are paid fairly beside others. Workers’ rights campaigners say the measure will particularly help young people and women seek more equal pay. Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said anyone who has searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read “competitive salary.” Experts say leaving pay off an advert makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to offer lower pay to some candidates, including women. Burnham has used his early months for smaller changes, including removing VAT from electricity bills, reducing bus fares, and a 100-pound council-tax rebate, while he works on a 10-year plan he says is aimed at ending what he calls 40 years of neoliberalism. He said this week that plan’s publication could be delayed until next year, having originally been expected next month. Ministers consulted in July on equal-pay changes and have not yet set final plans for greater protections for disabled people and ethnic minorities. They have promised further policy changes to help young people into work after a review by former minister Alan Milburn, due in the coming weeks. The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found that less than half of employers always publish salary ranges, and less than a fifth always publish a specific salary. The government said 93 percent of businesses responded positively to the consultation; ministers have not yet decided what must be published, which size of company must comply, or how the rule will be enforced.
Ranks: jobseekers and workers across Britain · pay hidden on ads would have to be shown · announced, not yet in force Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov/06/uk-employers-forced-put-salaries-job-adverts-andy-burnham)

**Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say: BBC**
In France, one child and one young adult died after a bus crashed on Friday in Lent, in the east of the country, local authorities told the BBC. The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse and crashed at about 7 a.m. local time, about 34 miles, or 55 kilometres, from the Swiss border. Mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus left the road and hit a tree in a ditch. He told BFM TV he arrived minutes after the crash, that people were in shock, and that the side of the bus was torn off, so those seated on that side must have been seriously hurt. The Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor’s office said the bus carried 43 passengers, including 15 children; three people are in a critical condition and a further 13 have sustained minor injuries. The driver was taken to hospital with injuries and has not yet been questioned by police, the prosecutor’s office said. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said the crash involved students, and told reporters it is always difficult when children are victims of accidents of this nature. Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot, on his way to the area, said more than 100 firefighters had been sent. Emergency services were at the scene, and medical helicopters took the seriously injured to a specialised hospital. The mayor said the local town hall was opened to shelter people and to coordinate with those services. Photos in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in a roadside ditch, trees along the road, and heavy damage to the front.
Ranks: 43 passengers and their families in eastern France · two dead, three critical · Friday morning Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly00l4p3lwo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Pollution, shortages, crime: Daily life in Pakistan's megacity Karachi: France 24**
In Pakistan, residents of Karachi blocked several major roads in recent days after hours of power cuts, France 24 reports. The city has more than 21 million people and is the country’s economic hub, home to a large share of its businesses, jobs, and wealth. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s 2026 Global Liveability Index ranks Karachi 170th of 173 cities, ahead of only Dhaka, Tripoli, and Damascus. France 24 calls that a striking contrast for the economic powerhouse. The city receives only about 55 percent of the water it needs. In some neighbourhoods, power cuts can last up to 19 hours a day. It generates nearly 15,000 tonnes of waste every day, and almost a quarter of that never reaches a landfill. Residents also face crippling traffic congestion, inadequate public transport, crime, and chronic shortages of basic services. Despite several major urban development projects in recent years, France 24 says the infrastructure is struggling to keep pace with rapid growth. The report is by Sonia Ghezali, Shahzaib Wahlah, Ondine de Gaulle, and Jamil Iqbal.
Ranks: more than 21 million Karachi residents · water, power, and waste short every day · already, with protests this week Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/focus/20261106-pollution-shortages-crime-daily-life-in-pakistan-s-megacity-karachi)

**California governor says commuting all death sentences in state: France 24**
California Governor Gavin Newsom said Thursday he was commuting every death sentence in the state to life imprisonment, a move France 24 reports will affect more than 500 prisoners.
Ranks: more than 500 people on California’s death row · death sentences changed to life · announced Thursday Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261106-california-governor-says-commuting-all-death-sentences-in-state)

**Mexico’s central bank cuts rates to 6.25% in surprise split decision: London Daily News**
Mexico’s central bank cut its key interest rate to 6.25 percent in a surprise split decision.
Ranks: borrowers and savers across Mexico · a lower policy rate · the decision already taken Source: [londondaily.news](https://www.londondaily.news/mexicos-central-bank-cuts-rates-to-6-25-in-surprise-split-decision/)

**Saudi-Led Forces Bombed Yemeni Home, Killing Nine Family Members, Relatives Say: The New York Times**
Relatives say a Saudi-led, U.S.-assisted bombing of a Yemeni home in October killed nine members of one family, in the campaign against the Houthis.
Ranks: one Yemeni family, and civilians in that campaign · nine killed · the October strike, reported now Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/world/middleeast/saudi-arabia-bombing-yemen-civilians-houthi-war.html)

**European skies on high alert after hoax bomb threats this week: The Guardian**
France’s prime minister’s office said four new bomb threats against aircraft over French territory arrived today; every plane landed safely, and bomb disposal units are inspecting them while a probe looks for the origin.
Ranks: passengers on those flights, and European aviation · searches after safe landings · today Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/06/high-alert-hoax-bomb-threats-france-air-lingus-belgium-pope-leo-europe-live)

**Court grants ex-Malaysian PM Najib house arrest after $12m royal pardon: Al Jazeera**
A Malaysian court granted former prime minister Najib house arrest after a 12-million-dollar royal pardon, once his party paid the fine through crowdfunding.
Ranks: Najib and Malaysia’s courts · custody moved from prison to house arrest · the court has approved it Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6/courts-grant-ex-malaysian-pm-najib-house-arrest-after-12m-royal-pardon?traffic_source=rss)

### Both Sides: Denmark’s “non-western” housing classification
Denmark’s supreme court is expected to rule on whether the state’s classification of residents with “non-western” backgrounds is covered by racial discrimination law, in an appeal by people evicted from the Nøjsomhed-Sydvej housing complex in Helsingør, north of Copenhagen. The Guardian reports that the case could reach others forced out under legislation once known as the ghetto law, which the government now describes as a policy on “parallel societies.”

The residents’ case, as the appeal frames it, is that the classification itself is the harm: they were removed from their homes under a rule that sorts people by a “non-western” background, and they are asking the supreme court to decide that this sorting falls under racial discrimination law. Their strongest reason, on the facts the court has been given, is that the label is what put them in the class of people who could be evicted, so ethnicity is not incidental to the removal.

The government’s case is that the removal of the former residents of that Helsingør complex is unrelated to their ethnicity. Its strongest reason, as stated, is that the policy is about neighbourhoods it calls parallel societies, not about the ethnic identity of the people who lived there.

What happens next is the supreme court’s ruling on whether that classification is covered by racial discrimination law. A finding that the classification is covered would bear on others already forced out under the same legislation; a finding that it is not would leave those evictions standing on the government’s stated ground.

# Omni View Top World News
> **Forty-two are dead after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian aid centre, with dozens still missing.**

Bomb threats diverted flights across Europe, France is braced for a national day of strikes, and Yemen's month-old government offensive has settled into attrition. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Dozens dead and missing after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid centre: France 24**
In Ukraine, officials say the death toll from a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region has risen to 42. Dozens of people are still missing, the same officials said. France 24 describes the strike as one of the deadliest on civilians this year. The bombing was on Monday. It struck people gathered at a point where aid was being handed out, not a military position named in the report. The attack came a day after a brief US-brokered local ceasefire expired. Less than a week on, the United States is due to bring Ukrainian and Russian delegations together in Abu Dhabi for talks on ending the war. That war is now in its fifth year. The talks are the next dated step the report names; the missing are still unaccounted for as the toll is given.
Ranks: Civilians at a Zaporizhzhia aid point, and negotiators due in Abu Dhabi · 42 dead and dozens missing · The dead are already counted; the talks are due within a week. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261105-dozens-dead-and-missing-after-russian-strike-on-ukrainian-aid-centre)

**New bomb threats bring fresh disruptions to flights across Europe: Al Jazeera**
Across Europe on Thursday, bomb threats forced about ten commercial flights into unplanned or high-alert landings, Al Jazeera's Frances Read said from London. An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to Evreux, west of Paris, escorted by French military aircraft, and landed safely. The office of Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said it was monitoring the incident in real time, that a bomb squad was in place, and that 151 passengers and six crew were moved to safety. No one claimed responsibility, and officials did not attribute blame. In Bulgaria, Ryanair flights from Copenhagen and Madrid landed in Sofia under alert, and a Ryanair service from London Stansted diverted to Plovdiv, the airport's chief executive said. Czech police said four planes bound for Prague had been threatened with improvised explosive devices, judged the relevance of the threats low, and still prepared pyrotechnic inspections after landing so the effect on passengers and operations would be as small as possible. A LOT flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at Zaventem after cabin crew found nothing suspicious and a further inspection found no dangerous items; the airport said no extra security measures were required. Wizz Air said a Milan-to-Warsaw flight diverted to Vienna after a hoax threat, and a separate Wizz Air service from Milan toward Bucharest was also listed among Thursday's alerts. A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted by a fighter jet and checked by bomb-disposal experts, while a threat against a Helsinki-to-Vienna flight, operated by Jettime, ended in a scheduled landing with no incident. Deutsche Welle reports the alerts follow threats earlier this week, including against LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair, that turned out to be hoaxes, and that no sign of dangerous materials had yet been reported on Thursday.
Ranks: Passengers and crews on about ten flights, plus airport staff in at least six countries · Diversions, escorts and searches, with no device reported so far · Thursday morning, and still unfolding. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5/bomb-threat-diverts-dublin-rome-flight-to-france?traffic_source=rss)
Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/several-european-flights-receive-bomb-threats-some-divert/a-79861216?maca=en-rss-en-world-4025-rdf)

**A month after Yemen government offensive began, war of attrition takes hold: Al Jazeera**
In Yemen, a month after the internationally recognised government launched Operation Dawn of Yemen on October 5, Sanaa is largely calm apart from recurring air strikes, while fighting has not stopped in the south. Government forces, backed by a Saudi Arabia-led coalition, said they aimed to retake all territory held by the Houthis, including the capital, which the Houthis have held since late 2014 after seizing it in the opening phase of a civil war now more than a decade old. Al Jazeera reports the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, have since scored territorial gains in Taiz and Lahij, where fighting has not ceased. The Yemeni government said last month that its forces killed or wounded 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours. Abdulsalam Mohammed, chairman of the Abaad Studies and Research Center, said the offensive forced the Houthis to move forces and equipment, exposing them to air strikes, and that many field commanders and hundreds of fighters were killed, especially in Taiz and on the western coast. He said those deaths have not stopped the territorial gains, but that the gains could be short-lived if government air power and ground forces keep attacking together. Turki al-Goblan, head of the Saudi Daimumah Center for Studies, said the offensive has hit three pillars he described as Houthi fuel and supply lines, maritime routes around Bab al-Mandeb and the western coast, and reliance on tribes around Sanaa, some of which he said have begun mobilising for the recognised government. Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea and is a route for Saudi oil exports and for Asian goods bound for Europe. He argued the pace of attrition has outrun the Houthis' ability to replace losses, and that this is the more likely path to a decisive result. Mohammed Ahmed, a 40-year-old Sanaa resident, told Al Jazeera his fear was fighting inside the country's most densely populated city, and that the fear has eased as the capital stayed mostly quiet.
Ranks: Residents of Sanaa, Taiz and Lahij, and shipping through Bab al-Mandeb · A new phase of attrition, with disputed ground and a government casualty claim · Ongoing, one month into the offensive. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5/a-month-after-yemen-government-offensive-began-war-of-attrition-takes-hold?traffic_source=rss)

**Not just Congress: Democrats’ blue wave washes over state legislatures across US: The Guardian**
In the United States, Democrats gained hundreds of state legislative seats in Tuesday's midterm elections, The Guardian reports. Ballots are still being counted. The paper says the party's success appears historic, and that the wins were under the radar beside the congressional result. It reports Democrats have not held full control of government in Arizona in 60 years, in Pennsylvania since the 1990s, or in Wisconsin since their wipeout in 2010. In Michigan and Minnesota, The Guardian reports, they regained trifectas they lost after the 2024 election. In Texas, it reports, they will control the state house for the first time since 2002. The Guardian says those chamber wins may have major implications for daily life, because state legislatures write much of the law people actually live under. It also says the party is set to embark on an aggressive legislative spree once the new majorities are seated. The count is not finished, so the paper presents the scale as what the returns so far appear to show, not as a final national tally of seats.
Ranks: Residents of states where legislative control changed, including Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota and Texas · Who writes state law · As counts finish, and for the coming legislative terms. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/05/democrats-state-legislatures-midterm-elections)

**How elderly ‘unsung heroes’ powered Lula’s historic fightback in Brazil: The Guardian**
In Brazil, The Guardian reports that older voters helped President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva overturn a first-round loss in the October 25 runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula lost the October 4 first round. More than 1 million elderly people who missed that round voted in the second, among them Celia de Oliveira Soares, 101, who had not voted in nearly a decade and cast number 13 for Lula. Never since the return of democracy in the 1980s had a first-round loser come back, and Lula did, The Guardian reports, finding 10.3 million extra votes between the rounds. Of 3 million extra voters who skipped the first round and took part in the second, 1.4 million were over 70. Voting is mandatory in Brazil only for people aged 18 to 69, so the over-70 turnout was voluntary. Political journalist José Roberto de Toledo said turnout was measurably higher among older voters, particularly those aged 60 to 79, and that images of people in their 80s, 90s and 100s being carried to polling stations matched a statistical movement rather than a staged one. The Guardian lists other explanations still being weighed by election experts: a sharp rise in welfare benefits on the eve of the vote, a pro-Lula WhatsApp group that grew from 50,000 to nearly 11 million members in less than a month, and street protests it describes as involving millions. At his 81st birthday party, Lula himself credited elderly voters who reached polling stations with walking frames, sticks, stretchers and wheelchairs. At a victory celebration, former minister Simone Tebet called the result a cross-generational triumph and said young people hit the streets while older voters saved democracy.
Ranks: Brazil's electorate, including more than a million older people who voted only in the runoff · A completed presidential result, with 10.3 million extra second-round votes · Already decided on October 25. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/05/unsung-heroes-behind-lula-surprise-election-triumph-brazil-runoff-bolsonaro)

More than 220 demonstrations are expected across France on Thursday as five unions join a national day of action over the cost of living.
Ranks: People across France facing strikes and marches · A national day of action after weeks of protests · Thursday. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/world/europe/france-protests-general-strike.html)

In Ethiopia, a renewed conflict has displaced thousands, and humanitarian groups have all but left many camps short of food and health care.

In Serbia, ten suspects are accused of abusing and torturing protesters in a Belgrade government-compound garage.

### Both Sides: Should the United States end the Iran war now?
The question is whether Washington should end the Iran war now, after Republicans lost control of Congress. Vice President JD Vance makes the case for treating the war as the loss that has to be faced. He wrote on Wednesday that the reason the party lost is the war, and that the president himself said so the night before. He asked anyone who believes losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it to argue that case. Citing an unnamed pollster, he said that ending the Iran war and changing the relationship with Israel were among the top four answers given, ahead of this week's midterms, by Americans who voted for the Republican ticket in 2024 and planned to vote Democratic this year. President Donald Trump makes the case for continuing until a nuclear bar is locked in. IranWire reports that on Wednesday he said what the United States did with Iran had to be done and is continuing, and that the conflict was worth the political cost of losing congressional control. He said he can end the war whenever he wants, but that it has to be done right, so Iran can never resume a nuclear program after American forces withdraw. Al Jazeera reports he told The Wall Street Journal, "I did the right thing. I would have done it again," about launching the war alongside Israel in February, and told reporters that Vance was largely right that higher fuel prices turned voters, while insisting the war was necessary to stop a nuclear weapon. Senator Ted Cruz, speaking from a hawkish position rather than an end-it-now one, said the war should have been brief, decisive and over, that it dragged on too long, and that Washington should never give the Iranian leadership billions of dollars. Al Jazeera tied that remark to a 300-billion-dollar rebuild fund discussed in a June memorandum of understanding that quickly fell apart. Iran's parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said Americans used their votes to say no to war. No end date is set. Trump's stated condition is a withdrawal that leaves Iran unable to restart a nuclear program. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5/congress-defeat-how-trumps-allies-are-distancing-themselves-from-iran-war?traffic_source=rss)

# Omni View Top World News
> **Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, reshaping Trump's final two years.**

**What You Need to Know:** Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, reshaping Donald Trump's final two years in office. Persian Gulf governments warned that another US-Iran war would be more destructive, while a Houthi siege has encircled Yemen's Taiz for 30 days. This edition also draws on the Omni View Omni View North America desk.

### The Ten
**Democrats win control of House and Senate: Key US midterms takeaways: Al Jazeera**
In the United States, Democrats have won both the Senate and the House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency, which France 24 described as his final two years. Not every seat is called. Al Jazeera, citing the Associated Press, reported Democrats on 228 House seats and leading in 34 more, a total that could pass 260 and would be their largest House strength since 1990, when they won 267; after the 2024 election Republicans held 220 House seats and Democrats 215. In the Senate, Democrats have won 54 seats and lead in another, while Republicans have won 44 and lead in one; control takes 51, and Democrats last had a majority this clear in 2008, when they won 56. It is the first time in 20 years a Republican president has lost both houses, after George W. Bush in 2006, and Democrats have already flipped 25 House seats, more than the 21 they took in 2008, including seats in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, Michigan and Kansas. Al Jazeera also reported 28 Democratic governors to 20 Republicans, with two races uncalled, against 27 Republican and 23 Democratic governors after 2024. Hakeem Jeffries told supporters, "Today begins the great American comeback"; if colleagues keep him as House leader, he would be the first Black Speaker, succeeding Republican Mike Johnson. Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, defeated Mike Rogers in Michigan and is the first Muslim elected to the US Senate; he is to be sworn in on January 3. Trump called him a "jihadist" without citing evidence, and El-Sayed told supporters they could turn "inshallah" into "alhamdulillah," adding, "For the right-wing ops, that just means 'praise be to God.'" Susan Collins, Republican senator for Maine for three decades, conceded to Democrat Troy Jackson and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve 30 years. Trump said Democrats did a "good job," that he would accept the results, and that "Iran was a piece of it," while noting he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation; he also said that in some cases Republican candidates "were not my friend." Voters decided 145 ballot questions in more than three dozen states: Missouri rejected a proposed amendment that would have limited most abortions, with the Associated Press putting the "no" vote at 55.5 percent, and rejected a 2025 congressional map with 61.8 percent voting no; Virginia wrote in a right to reproductive freedom covering the first two trimesters, and Nevada a right to abortion until fetal viability, generally after 21 weeks, while Idaho defeated a measure that would have created abortion rights in state law. France 24 reported Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of Georgia, and Byron Donalds the first Black man elected governor of Florida.
Ranks: US voters and anyone bound by federal law, war policy and trade · who controls Congress, investigations and the veto fight · immediately, for the rest of this presidency Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4/democrats-win-control-of-house-and-senate-key-us-midterms-takeaways?traffic_source=rss) · [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmr4y92rgd9po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) · [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261104-us-voters-back-abortion-rights-and-reject-trump-s-gerrymandering-in-state-ballot-measures) · [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/press-review/20261104-blue-tsunami-in-us-midterms-pummels-gop-out-of-power) · [komu.com](https://www.komu.com/news/elections/missouri-2026-midterm-election-results-key-races-and-amendments/article_bfd35c26-3fac-4a11-8265-261b8410d127.html) · [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4/rejecting-hate-abdul-el-sayed-wins-senate-seat-despite-racist-attacks?traffic_source=rss)

**Persian Gulf leaders fear a renewed U.S.-Iran war as diplomacy sputters: Los Angeles Times**
In Bahrain, diplomats at the Manama Dialogue warned that another round of fighting between the United States and Iran could be more destructive than the war the Los Angeles Times said began on February 28. Anwar Gargash, a presidential adviser in the United Arab Emirates, said the Iranian and American stands are far apart and that "if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst," adding that regional states are seeking a "political offramp" in a "protracted crisis of no war, no peace." Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said governments must "push very hard in order to prevent the escalation," because a second round "will be more dangerous, more destructive and it will lead to nowhere," and because more fighting would affect food and energy security. President Trump has hinted he could launch "another little Operation Epic Fury" after Tuesday's midterms, referring to the US-Israeli operation that opened the war, but on Monday he wrote, "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!" Hours later, Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Associated Press quoted an unnamed US official saying the military had carried out "defensive strikes." The Times reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, after an inconclusive election last month, is said to be pressing Trump to finish off the Islamic Republic. Last week Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials flew to Tehran and met Iranian military officials; Qatar is leading talks on a de-escalation plan Tehran has presented and Trump has not accepted. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the Islamic Republic News Agency it is up to the Americans to decide "whether they have the will to take the wise path of diplomacy or, as in the past, seek to drag the situation into aggression and military operations." He added, "If they dare to test us again," they "will receive a much more bitter and severe result than before," after a first round in which Iran struck American bases in the region with drones and cruise and ballistic missiles.
Ranks: people in Iran, Israel and the Gulf, plus food and energy buyers · whether talks hold or a second round starts · days to weeks, with strikes already reported Source: [latimes.com](https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-11-04/persian-gulf-leaders-fear-renewed-u-s-iran-war-as-diplomacy-sputters)

**Houthis’ monthlong siege on Taiz creating hell for trapped Yemenis: Al Jazeera**
In Yemen, the Houthis' siege of Taiz has lasted 30 days and, Al Jazeera reported, has affected hundreds of thousands of people. The United Nations has repeatedly warned of a catastrophe inside the city, where food and medicine are becoming scarce. The blockade has affected the 1.5 million people in Taiz City and others in rural districts, including about 180,000 displaced people trapped by clashes along the main road between Lahj and Taiz. The siege tightened when the Houthis seized al-Turbah, in the far southwest of the governorate, cutting the city's main artery to Aden. The Houthis reached Taiz's outskirts in 2015 after pushing the government out of Sanaa in September 2014; their takeover of the western countryside has now encircled the city. Salah Ahmed Ghaleb al-Majidi, acting director of the governorate's Siege Affairs Department, called it "the worst catastrophic siege imposed on a Yemeni city since the war began in 2014," with food, fuel, medical supplies and water not reaching the city and rubbish piling up. He said cut roads are also keeping families from relatives. Ahmed al-Mikhlafi, whose name Al Jazeera shortened for security, returned from Umrah in Mecca to find himself stuck in the western countryside; he described nearly 20 new Houthi checkpoints and a stop about 15 kilometres from the city, where fighters ordered his vehicle to turn back because of clashes.
Ranks: about 1.5 million people in Taiz City, plus rural residents and about 180,000 displaced people · food, fuel, medicine, water and movement cut · now, one month into the siege Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4/houthis-one-month-siege-on-taiz-is-creating-hell-for-yemenis-stuck-there?traffic_source=rss)

**Netanyahu’s political rivals seize on Democrats’ sweep, seeking his ouster: The Globe and Mail**
In Israel, a week after an election the Globe and Mail described as leaving Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition without a parliamentary majority, his rivals seized on the Democratic capture of Congress as proof he had squandered generations of bipartisan American support. The same account said the coalition still performed well enough to deny his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, a clear path to unseat him. Unlike earlier Israeli leaders who courted both US parties, Netanyahu has openly backed Republicans. The Globe and Mail reported that support for Israel among Democrats and some Republicans wavered after Israel's assault in Gaza following the 2023 Hamas attack, and fell further after Trump and Netanyahu ordered a joint attack on Iran. Some Democratic candidates made criticism of American military aid to Israel a campaign argument. Trump, who had endorsed Netanyahu, made an election-day pledge to halt 4 billion US dollars in annual funding to Israel, which he said would take away a "bad talking point" used by Democrats. Yair Golan, head of the centre-left Democrats party, wrote that the US results "reveal just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans." Yair Lapid said "Israel cannot afford" for Netanyahu to remain, because "It endangers our security, it jeopardises our democracy, and it will ruin our standing on the global stage." Netanyahu has so far remained silent on the US vote.
Ranks: Israelis waiting on a government, and the US-Israel aid relationship · who can form a cabinet, plus a pledged halt to 4 billion dollars a year · now, with coalition talks unresolved Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-us-midterm-election-results-live-updates-november-4-2026/)

**30 million South Africans registered to vote across nine provinces: France 24**
In South Africa, local elections are being held on Wednesday across nine provinces. About 30 million people have registered to cast votes, France 24 reported. The economy is at the forefront of the election. The spotlight is on Gauteng, a province long plagued by governance challenges. Helen Zille, 75, is running for mayor of Johannesburg. The New York Times reported she is betting voters care less about race and more about public services. The Times also reported that she is needling the African National Congress in that bid. No result is in; the polls are the decision, not a forecast.
Ranks: about 30 million registered voters in South Africa · who runs local services, including in Johannesburg and Gauteng · votes being cast today Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261104-30-million-south-africans-registered-to-vote-across-nine-provinces) · [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/world/africa/johannesburg-mayor-elections.html)

**EU to lead talks on support for Ukraine with US, Nato, partners: The Guardian**
The European Commission will meet the United States, Nato and the World Bank on winter aid after strikes hit Kyiv, Zhytomyr and a vessel near Odesa.
Ranks: people in Ukraine facing winter · power stations and a cargo ship hit, aid talks opening · immediate Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/04/eu-ukraine-russia-france-germany-us-nato-europe-latest-news)

**US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters: BBC**
An Ethiopian-born American admitted sharing dozens of classified US documents with senior Ethiopian officials to help kill Tigray fighters.
Ranks: US secrecy rules and the record of Ethiopia's Tigray war · dozens of classified documents admitted shared · already admitted Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y8lz73vmv7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**U.K. Supreme Court Hears Challenge to Ban on Palestine Action: What to Know: The New York Times**
Britain's Supreme Court hears a challenge today to last year's designation of Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation.
Ranks: members and critics of Palestine Action, and UK protest law · whether the ban stands · the hearing is today Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/world/europe/palestine-action-ban-uk-supreme-court.html)

**Azerbaijan's central bank reserves rise 35.7% y/y to $15.4bn: IntelliNews**
Azerbaijan's central bank reserves rose 35.7 percent in a year, to 15.4 billion dollars.
Ranks: Azerbaijan's public finances · reserves up by more than a third · already recorded, year on year Source: [intellinews.com](https://www.intellinews.com/azerbaijan-s-central-bank-reserves-rise-35-7-y-y-to-15-4bn-481604/)

**Euro zone wage growth to rebound slightly next year, ECB says: Yahoo Finance**
The European Central Bank says euro zone wage growth will rebound slightly next year.
Ranks: euro zone workers and employers · a slight rebound the ECB projects · next year Source: [finance.yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/euro-zone-wage-growth-rebound-093415154.html)

### Both Sides: Should the NBA keep Rwanda's paid partnership while US military sanctions stand?
The question is whether the National Basketball Association should keep a paid partnership with Rwanda, including finals at Kigali's BK Arena, while United States sanctions on Rwanda's military remain. The army-funded APR club has already been withdrawn from the 2026 Basketball Africa League. Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn wrote on 23 October that the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights," and asked, "What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" Their best reason is that a league that speaks of justice cannot keep taking government money after Washington sanctioned the Rwandan army in March, accusing it of fuelling the war in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and last week sanctioned the defence ministry over support for the M23 group, which has seized large parts of the east. DR Congo has asked the NBA, European clubs and Formula 1 to end Rwandan campaigns, arguing the deals clean Rwanda's image while fighting continues. NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the team "had been withdrawn" after those earlier sanctions, and the club stays barred while the sanctions last. Rwanda's stated case is a denial: Rwanda denies backing the rebels. That denial, if accepted, undercuts the charge that the partnership launders a war role. What is not in dispute in the reporting is the commercial fact: Rwanda is an official league partner, has hosted all but one final and playoff series since 2021 in the 10,000-seat arena, and the NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars a year. APR, third in 2024 and 2025, was replaced this year by the RSSB Tigers. The senators' 2 November deadline for a written answer has passed. The team remains out for as long as the sanctions stand; the articles do not set a date for ending or keeping the Kigali finals. Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699zdx9knmpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

### Progress Watch
In Kenya, Food4Education now serves more than 600,000 school meals a day across 19,000 schools, with parents in some cases paying 5 Kenyan shillings, about 3 US cents, and about 80 percent of the food coming from small-scale farmers. DW reported that data show children at participating schools miss fewer classes and perform better, and that founder Wawira Njiru, 35, is receiving this year's German Africa Prize; the organisation has 6,000 staff, more than 70 percent of them women. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/wawira-njiru-kenya-s-no-1-school-feeder-honored-with-the-german-africa-prize/a-79646537?maca=en-rss-en-world-4025-rdf)
